title: AIR-LLM: Broadcasting AI Weights over Radio for Memory-Free Edge LLM Inference via RF Computing
byline:
Zhihui Gao

Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA

Abstract.

Next-generation large language models (LLMs) are expanding from the cloud to ubiquitous edge devices. However, edge devices typically either lack the memory to store increasingly large LLM weights or, even with enough memory, spend unaffordable energy on loading the weights. This raises our question: can an edge device run an LLM without storing or loading its weights, but receive them over the air and consume them on the fly? Inspired by wireless broadcasting, we present AIR-LLM, an LLM inference architecture for edge devices, which is composed of: (i) a central radio (e.g., 5G base stations) that broadcasts the LLM weights into the air, and (ii) the edge user that receives the weights and completes the general matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) of LLM inference directly in the radio frequency (RF) domain using RF mixers. To further shorten the airtime, AIR-LLM exploits MIMO spatial multiplexing and proposes an energy-efficient precoder–postcoder pair on the edge to calibrate its own wireless channel. Since the central radio stays user-unaware, AIR-LLM is user-scalable so that one broadcast serves unlimited users within its coverage. We implement AIR-LLM on the NVIDIA Sionna ray-traced channels of two real-world urban scenes and the profiling of a real RF mixer. With a WikiText-2 perplexity degradation of 4.0% on LLaMA-3.1-8B, AIR-LLM saves the energy by 157.7×\times/40.4×\times against the FP16 and weight-only quantization baselines; with 20 users, its airtime is 104.1×\times/26.0×\times shorter, respectively.

Keywords: 

LLM inference, edge computing, RF computing, RF mixer, weight broadcasting, MIMO communication

1. Introduction

Trillions of edge devices today are embracing emerging machine learning (ML) techniques for a wide range of applications, such as continuous health monitoring (Abbaspourazad et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2025), on-device speech recognition (Radford et al., 2023; Yazdani et al., 2016), and cooperative autonomous driving (Hu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2021). Among these, the emerging large language models (LLMs) provide a unique capability, allowing understanding, reasoning, and generating natural language (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Touvron et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023; Gemma Team, 2026). However, the usage of LLMs on the edge mostly relies on cloud computing, where the locally generated prompts are uploaded to a cloud server, and the responses are downloaded afterwards. This again exposes two typical concerns of cloud computing: the privacy of the sensitive prompts, as well as the round-trip latency, especially when the number of edge users is scaled up (Kang et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2025).

The key challenge that hinders such an on-device deployment lies in the daunting model size of today’s LLMs. For example, LLaMA-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) occupies 16 GB in FP16, and still 4 GB after 4-bit weight-only quantization (WoQ) (Frantar et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024). Such a model size stresses an edge device in two stages. First, its memory is typically too small to hold the whole model, so a local deployment has to keep downloading the weights and discarding them afterwards. Second, even if an edge device could store such an LLM entirely, the energy of loading the weights from memory to the computing unit is unaffordable. This is because LLM inference is memory-bounded, especially during the decoding phase, where fetching one weight feeds only two floating-point operations (FLOPs) (Guo et al., 2025). The weight movement therefore dominates the energy, much more than the arithmetic it feeds (Antepara et al., 2025; NVIDIA, 2024).

To overcome this, various computing paradigms have been proposed recently. For example, in-memory computing completes the computing in analog within the memory itself, on a ReRAM (Shafiee et al., 2016; Chi et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2022), PCM (Khaddam-Aljameh et al., 2022; Le Gallo et al., 2023), or SRAM (Liu et al., 2026) crossbar, so that the weights are never fetched. Over-the-air computing (Nazer and Gastpar, 2007; Zhu et al., 2020), in turn, superposes the signals of many transmitters over the wireless channel, so that the summation is completed by the channel itself. However, in both cases the size of the general matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) is frozen and limited by the hardware complexity, e.g., a crossbar of 128×\times128 cells (Shafiee et al., 2016) and an array of a few dozen antennas (Reus-Muns et al., 2023). Such a limited GEMV size is naturally incompatible with the LLM whose GEMV sizes keep increasing.

Our motivation lies in the wireless network these edge users already live in. Taking 5G networks as an example, a 5G base station already establishes wireless links to each edge user under its coverage. For these users, accessing the LLM weights is read-only, and thus a purely downlink process; once they run the same LLM, it is exactly what broadcasting was invented for: one transmission simultaneously serving every user in the coverage. Moreover, we employ radio-frequency (RF) computing (Gao et al., 2026b; Gao et al., 2026a), which completes the computing in RF via the passive RF mixer that every receiver already carries. The computing is thereby finished in analog once the broadcast signal arrives, without the weights ever being digitized into the local memory.

As shown in Fig. 1, we present AIR-LLM, an LLM inference architecture with (i) a central radio (e.g., a 5G base station) that frequency-encodes the LLM weights onto the subcarriers of an orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) waveform and broadcasts it, and (ii) any edge device in the coverage receives that waveform and computes on it inside its own RF front-end. The key computing component is the RF mixer every wireless device already carries: it multiplies its two inputs in the time domain, corresponding to a linear convolution in the frequency domain. Specifically, driving its local oscillator (LO) with a waveform encoding the activations therefore convolves the arriving weight spectrum with the activation spectrum, and the very middle subcarrier of this convolution is exactly the inner product of the weight and activation vectors. A comparison of existing computing paradigms is presented in Tab. 1.

On top of this principle, AIR-LLM makes two designs. First, it exploits A×AA\times A multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) spatial multiplexing, which delivers AA weight streams at a time and thus shortens the airtime by A×A\times. Second, it calibrates the MIMO channel with CC calibration units, each pairing a per-subcarrier precoder and a per-antenna postcoder, which compensates for the channel at a cost far below an explicit inversion, keeping the energy low.

Delivering the weights this way also fits broadcasting better than conventional communication in two aspects. First, AIR-LLM needs no handshake with users, as the computation is inherently tolerant to the errors introduced by thermal noise. In addition, its weight waveform stays identical regardless of the users’ SNRs, so no per-user modulation and coding scheme (MCS) is needed either.

We implement AIR-LLM on ray-traced channels of two urban scenes, Paris and Munich, and profile a real RF mixer, running nine LLMs from 1B to 70B parameters end-to-end with every weight-activation GEMV in RF computing. On LLaMA-3.1-8B and a selected user in the scene of Paris, AIR-LLM degrades the WikiText-2 perplexity (PPL) by only 4.0%, while cutting the per-token energy by 157.7×\times/40.4×\times against FP16/4-bit weight baselines with remote weight storage, and by 51.5×\times/13.9×\times against fetching them from local memory; with 20 users, its per-token airtime is 104.1×\times/26.0×\times shorter than FP16 and 4-bit WoQ.

We summarize the contribution of AIR-LLM as below.

  • •

    We propose AIR-LLM, a new computing paradigm for LLM inference on the edge, which is memory-access-free, user-scalable, and energy-efficient.

  • •

    We design an RF computing engine that shortens the airtime with MIMO spatial multiplexing, while maintaining the computing accuracy and energy efficiency.

  • •

    We evaluate AIR-LLM on Sionna ray-tracing and real RF mixer profiling, showing its near-lossless PPL on LLM tasks with orders-of-magnitude less energy and airtime.

2. Preliminaries

2.1. OFDM and MIMO Channel Model

OFDM signal structure.   The signals are based on orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM), characterized by the FFT size NfftN_{\textrm{fft}}, i.e., the number of subcarriers in the frequency domain, and the occupied bandwidth BB. The resulting subcarrier spacing is Δ​f=B/Nfft\Delta f=B/N_{\textrm{fft}}.

MIMO signal notation.   We consider an At×ArA^{t}\times A^{r} MIMO system, where AtA^{t} denotes the number of transmitting antennas on the central radio and ArA^{r} denotes the number of receiving antennas on each edge device. On the central radio side, the transmitted signals in the frequency domain are denoted by a complex-valued matrix St∈ℂAt×NfftS^{t}\in\mathbb{C}^{A^{t}\times N_{\textrm{fft}}}, whose ata^{t}-th row St[at,:]S^{t}[a^{t},:] gives the signal transmitted by the ata^{t}-th antenna. The received signals in the frequency domain are similarly denoted by Sr∈ℂAr×NfftS^{r}\in\mathbb{C}^{A^{r}\times N_{\textrm{fft}}}, whose ara^{r}-th row Sr[ar,:]S^{r}[a^{r},:] gives the signal received by the ara^{r}-th antenna.

Wireless channel and received signal.   The wireless channel is defined as a three-dimensional complex-valued matrix H∈ℂAt×Ar×NfftH\in\mathbb{C}^{A^{t}\times A^{r}\times N_{\textrm{fft}}}, where H[at,ar,:]H[a^{t},a^{r},:] is the channel response between the ata^{t}-th transmitting antenna and the ara^{r}-th receiving antenna across all subcarriers. The received signal is then given by

(1) Sr​[ar,k]=∑at=0At−1H⁡[at,ar,k]⋅St​[at,k]+σNfft⋅𝒩,\displaystyle S^{r}[a^{r},k]=\sum_{a^{t}=0}^{A^{t}-1}H[a^{t},a^{r},k]\cdot S^{t}[a^{t},k]+\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{N_{\textrm{fft}}}}\cdot\mathcal{N},

where σ2\sigma^{2} is the sum power of the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) across all the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} subcarriers, and 𝒩\mathcal{N} is the i.i.d. complex-valued standard Gaussian distribution. Note that we assume that within a single edge device, the noise power is identical for all the antennas and subcarriers. Conventionally, the channel HH can either be pre-calibrated on the central radio side or post-calibrated on the edge device side. Specifically for the edge-side post-calibration, given the estimated channel H^\widehat{H}, a per-subcarrier (pseudo-)inverse matrix is performed for each H^[:,:,k]\widehat{H}[:,:,k] to recover the transmitted signal by

(2) St^[:,k]=(H^[:,:,k])−1⋅Sr[:,k].\displaystyle\widehat{S^{t}}[:,k]=\left(\widehat{H}[:,:,k]\right)^{-1}\cdot S^{r}[:,k].

This recovery process requires 8​At​Ar​Nfft8A^{t}A^{r}N_{\textrm{fft}} floating-point operations (FLOPs) on the edge device.

2.2. Analog GEMV via RF Mixers

An RF mixer is a fundamental component on edge devices for up/down conversion. Essentially, it performs analog multiplication in the time domain, corresponding to the linear convolution in the frequency domain, where OFDM signals reside. Such a convolution operation can be leveraged for GEMV in ML inference.

Complex-valued linear convolution.   The complex-valued nature of wireless signals allows an RF mixer to perform, in analog, the complex-valued linear convolution (denoted by ∗\ast) between two input signals of equal subcarrier spacing Δ​f\Delta f. To simplify, we assume they have the same FFT size (NfftN_{\textrm{fft}}) so that we denote the frequency-domain input activation signal by X∈ℂNfftX\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\textrm{fft}}}, and the weight signal by W∈ℂNfftW\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\textrm{fft}}}. This process yields the output activation signal Y∈ℂ2​Nfft−1Y\in\mathbb{C}^{2N_{\textrm{fft}}-1} as

(3) Y⁡[k]=(W∗X)​[k]=∑k′W⁡[k′]⋅X⁡[k−k′].\displaystyle Y[k]=\left(W\ast X\right)[k]=\sum_{k^{\prime}}W[k^{\prime}]\cdot X[k-k^{\prime}].

Leveraging linear convolution for GEMVs/IPs.   We examine the real-valued GEMV that ML inference is built upon, formulated by 𝐘=𝐖⋅𝐗\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{W}\cdot\mathbf{X} with 𝐖∈ℝM×N\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}, 𝐗∈ℝN\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}, and 𝐘∈ℝM\mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{M}. This GEMV can be broken down into MM independent NN-element inner products (IPs), each of which takes 2​N−12N-1 FLOPs. Since the linear convolution in (3) is complex-valued whereas the GEMV is real-valued, a single pair of input and weight signals carries two such IPs. Specifically, for the IP pair given by the mm-th and the m′m^{\prime}-th rows of 𝐖\mathbf{W}, we let the FFT size be Nfft=NN_{\textrm{fft}}=N, and let the input signal directly carry 𝐗\mathbf{X}, whereas the weight signal carries these two rows in its real and imaginary parts, both in a reversed subcarrier order, i.e.,

X⁡[k]\displaystyle X[k] =𝐗⁡[k],\displaystyle=\mathbf{X}[k],
(4) Wm,m′​[k]\displaystyle W_{m,m^{\prime}}[k] =𝐖⁡[m,N−1−k]+j⋅𝐖⁡[m′,N−1−k].\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}[m,N-1-k]+{j}\cdot\mathbf{W}[m^{\prime},N-1-k].

Substituting (4) into (3), the middle subcarrier of the output signal, Y⁡[N−1]Y[N-1], is exactly the one that accumulates all the NN element-wise products, i.e.,

Ym,m′​[N−1]\displaystyle Y_{m,m^{\prime}}[N-1] =∑k=0N−1(𝐖⁡[m,k]+j⋅𝐖⁡[m′,k])⋅𝐗⁡[k]\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\left(\mathbf{W}[m,k]+{j}\cdot\mathbf{W}[m^{\prime},k]\right)\cdot\mathbf{X}[k]
(5) =𝐘⁡[m]+j⋅𝐘⁡[m′],\displaystyle=\mathbf{Y}[m]+{j}\cdot\mathbf{Y}[m^{\prime}],

so that the two IPs are read off the real and the imaginary parts of this same subcarrier without interfering with each other, while the remaining 2​N−22N-2 subcarriers are discarded. Therefore, the output can be extracted by a low-pass filter (LPF) of a single-subcarrier bandwidth Δ​f\Delta f so that it can be digitized with far fewer samples to save the energy consumption on the ADCs. This process is repeated until all the MM IPs are covered, taking ⌈M/2⌉\left\lceil{M/2}\right\rceil weight signals Wm,m′W_{m,m^{\prime}} in total, all sharing the same input signal XX.

Beyond GEMV, this linear convolution maps even more naturally onto convolutional layers (Appendix D.1) (Gao et al., 2026a).

3. RF Computing Engine

In this section, we present the RF computing engine of AIR-LLM on the edge device based on MIMO, as shown in Fig. 2, where AIR-LLM calibrates the channel of the broadcast weights with a pair of precoder and postcoder that are compatible with the RF mixer-driven analog GEMV.

3.1. Problem Formulation

We first introduce the basic configuration of the MIMO channel modeling, and then formulate the problem of designing the edge device hardware.

GEMV decoupling and IP parallelization.   In AIR-LLM, we consider an A×AA\times A MIMO system for any central radio and edge device pair. This supports up to AA parallel spatial streams, each carrying an IP pair of (4), so that one round of AIR-LLM completes 2​A2A IPs and a GEMV takes ⌈M/(2​A)⌉\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil rounds. For these 2​A2A IPs per round, we denote the weight signals by 𝐖={𝐰a}\mathbf{W}=\{\mathbf{w}_{a}\} and the shared input signal by 𝐱\mathbf{x}, all spanning the Nfft=NN_{\textrm{fft}}=N subcarriers, i.e., 𝐰a,𝐱∈ℂNfft\mathbf{w}_{a},\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\textrm{fft}}}; their outputs are denoted by 𝐘={𝐲a}\mathbf{Y}=\{\mathbf{y}_{a}\} with 𝐲a∈ℂ\mathbf{y}_{a}\in\mathbb{C}.

MIMO channel modeling.   In AIR-LLM, we let the central radio broadcast signals 𝐖\mathbf{W} with 𝐰a\mathbf{w}_{a} by the aa-th antenna without precoding. For a specific edge device with a channel H∈ℂA×A×NfftH\in\mathbb{C}^{A\times A\times N_{\textrm{fft}}}, the received signals are denoted by 𝐖′={𝐰a′}\mathbf{W}^{\prime}=\{\mathbf{w}^{\prime}_{a}\} with 𝐰a′∈ℂNfft\mathbf{w}^{\prime}_{a}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\textrm{fft}}} received by the aa-th antenna. This signal transmission process directly follows the MIMO channel model in (1), with At=Ar=AA^{t}=A^{r}=A.

Channel calibration challenges.   The design of the central radio is edge device-unaware, i.e., does not incorporate any information specific to a particular edge device (e.g., its channel), so that its broadcasting can be generalized for any edge device within its coverage. In this case, the channel effect on 𝐖\mathbf{W} should be entirely calibrated at the edge device side. However, the conventional channel calibration in (2) is not feasible for AIR-LLM for two reasons. First, the channel effect applies to all the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} subcarriers of 𝐖\mathbf{W}, whereas the outputs 𝐘\mathbf{Y} are digitized only after the LPF has collapsed them into a single subcarrier, where the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} per-subcarrier channel matrices are already mixed together and no longer separable. Second, even if they were separable, applying (2) over the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} subcarriers would take 8​A2​Nfft8A^{2}N_{\textrm{fft}} FLOPs, approximately 2A×2A\times the cost of the 2​A2A IPs that it enables, overshadowing the energy savings that motivate AIR-LLM.

3.2. Edge Calibration Unit Design

We design the CC calibration units on the edge device to calibrate the channel effect, as shown in Fig. 3.

Calibration unit architecture.   Generally, a calibration unit takes the digital signal 𝐱\mathbf{x} as input, which is (i) precoded and IFFTed in digital, (ii) split and duplicated into AA ways in analog, (iii) respectively mixed with the analog received signals 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime} across the AA antennas and low-pass filtered, and (iv) postcoded in digital. The key design of this calibration unit is the precoding on the 𝐱\mathbf{x} and the postcoding on the 𝐘\mathbf{Y}.

Precoding for per-subcarrier calibration.   The precoding is performed on the input signal 𝐱\mathbf{x} to calibrate the non-flat frequency response of the channel. This is because 𝐱\mathbf{x} spans all the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} subcarriers, yet lacks any antenna-dimension information. Hereby, we define the precoder Ppre∈ℂNfftP_{\textrm{pre}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\textrm{fft}}}. Denoting the precoded signal by 𝐱′∈ℂNfft\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\textrm{fft}}}, the precoding process can be expressed as a per-subcarrier multiplication between 𝐱\mathbf{x} and PpreP_{\textrm{pre}}:

(6) 𝐱′[k]=𝐱[k]⋅Ppre[k],∀k=0,1,…,Nfft−1.\displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{\prime}[k]=\mathbf{x}[k]\cdot P_{\textrm{pre}}[k],\quad\forall k=0,1,\ldots,N_{\textrm{fft}}-1.

Precoded linear convolution in analog.   After the precoding, the input signal 𝐱′\mathbf{x}^{\prime} is split into AA ways and fed to the AA RF mixers, which perform the AA complex-valued convolutions in parallel against the respective received signals 𝐰a′\mathbf{w}^{\prime}_{a}, i.e.,

(7) 𝐲^a=𝐰′a⊤⋅𝐱′,∀a=0,1,…,A−1,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{a}={\mathbf{w}^{\prime}_{a}}^{\top}\cdot\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\quad\forall a=0,1,\ldots,A-1,

where 𝐲^a∈ℂ\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{a}\in\mathbb{C} is the unpostcoded output of antenna aa.

Postcoding for per-antenna calibration.   The postcoding is performed on the output signal 𝐘\mathbf{Y} to calibrate the inter-antenna interference. This is because 𝐘\mathbf{Y} retains the full antenna dimension, while its frequency dimension is already down-sampled and aliased. Specifically, we define the postcoder Ppost∈ℂA×AP_{\textrm{post}}\in\mathbb{C}^{A\times A}, which is applied identically across all subcarriers; also, we denote the postcoded output signals by 𝐘^′={𝐲^a′}\widehat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\prime}=\{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime}_{a}\} with 𝐲^a′∈ℂ\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime}_{a}\in\mathbb{C}. The postcoding process can be written as:

(8) 𝐲^a′=∑a′=0A−1Ppost​[a,a′]⋅𝐲^a′.\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime}_{a}=\sum_{a^{\prime}=0}^{A-1}P_{\textrm{post}}[a,a^{\prime}]\cdot\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{a^{\prime}}.

Cooperation over multiple calibration units.   We place CC such calibration units on the edge device, as shown in Fig. 3. Each calibration unit receives the same input signal 𝐱\mathbf{x} and the same received signals 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime} from the AA antennas, while applying a different precoder and postcoder, jointly denoted by Ppre∈ℂC×NfftP_{\textrm{pre}}\in\mathbb{C}^{C\times N_{\textrm{fft}}} and Ppost∈ℂC×A×AP_{\textrm{post}}\in\mathbb{C}^{C\times A\times A}. Correspondingly, the precoded input signals, unpostcoded outputs, and postcoded outputs are denoted by 𝐱c′\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_{c}, 𝐲^c,a\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{c,a}, and 𝐲^c,a′\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime}_{c,a}, respectively. Finally, the outputs from all the calibration units are summed together into the final output, denoted by 𝐘^′′={𝐲^a′′}\widehat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\prime\prime}=\{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime\prime}_{a}\} with 𝐲^a′′∈ℂ\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime\prime}_{a}\in\mathbb{C}, i.e.,

(9) 𝐲^′′a=∑c=0C−1𝐲^′c,a,∀a=0,1,…,A−1,\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime\prime}_{a}=\sum_{c=0}^{C-1}\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime}_{c,a},\quad\forall a=0,1,\dots,A-1,

3.3. Precoder and Postcoder Optimization

Putting (6), (7), (8), and (9) together, the ultimate goal of AIR-LLM is to minimize the mean squared error (MSE) between the final output signal 𝐲^′′\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime\prime} and the ground truth output signal 𝐲\mathbf{y} by optimizing the precoder PpreP_{\textrm{pre}} and postcoder PpostP_{\textrm{post}} jointly across all calibration units. We formulate this as the optimization problem in OPT-Orig.

Our motivation lies in the wireless network these edge users already live in. Taking 5G networks as an example, a 5G base station already establishes wireless links to each edge user under its coverage. For these users, accessing the LLM weights is read-only, and thus a purely downlink process; once they run the same LLM, it is exactly what broadcasting was invented for: one transmission simultaneously serving every user in the coverage. Moreover, we employ radio-frequency (RF) computing (Gao et al., 2026b; Gao et al., 2026a), which completes the computing in RF via the passive RF mixer that every receiver already carries. The computing is thereby finished in analog once the broadcast signal arrives, without the weights ever being digitized into the local memory. As shown in Fig. 1, we present AIR-LLM, an LLM inference architecture with (i) a central radio (e.g., a 5G base station) that frequency-encodes the LLM weights onto the subcarriers of an orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) waveform and broadcasts it, and (ii) any edge device in the coverage receives that waveform and computes on it inside its own RF front-end. The key computing component is the RF mixer every wireless device already carries: it multiplies its two inputs in the time domain, corresponding to a linear convolution in the frequency domain. Specifically, driving its local oscillator (LO) with a waveform encoding the activations therefore convolves the arriving weight spectrum with the activation spectrum, and the very middle subcarrier of this convolution is exactly the inner product of the weight and activation vectors. A comparison of existing computing paradigms is presented in Tab. 1. On top of this principle, AIR-LLM makes two designs. First, it exploits A×AA\times A multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) spatial multiplexing, which delivers AA weight streams at a time and thus shortens the airtime by A×A\times. Second, it calibrates the MIMO channel with CC calibration units, each pairing a per-subcarrier precoder and a per-antenna postcoder, which compensates for the channel at a cost far below an explicit inversion, keeping the energy low. Delivering the weights this way also fits broadcasting better than conventional communication in two aspects. First, AIR-LLM needs no handshake with users, as the computation is inherently tolerant to the errors introduced by thermal noise. In addition, its weight waveform stays identical regardless of the users’ SNRs, so no per-user modulation and coding scheme (MCS) is needed either. We implement AIR-LLM on ray-traced channels of two urban scenes, Paris and Munich, and profile a real RF mixer, running nine LLMs from 1B to 70B parameters end-to-end with every weight-activation GEMV in RF computing. On LLaMA-3.1-8B and a selected user in the scene of Paris, AIR-LLM degrades the WikiText-2 perplexity (PPL) by only 4.0%, while cutting the per-token energy by 157.7×\times/40.4×\times against FP16/4-bit weight baselines with remote weight storage, and by 51.5×\times/13.9×\times against fetching them from local memory; with 20 users, its per-token airtime is 104.1×\times/26.0×\times shorter than FP16 and 4-bit WoQ. We summarize the contribution of AIR-LLM as below. • We propose AIR-LLM, a new computing paradigm for LLM inference on the edge, which is memory-access-free, user-scalable, and energy-efficient. • We design an RF computing engine that shortens the airtime with MIMO spatial multiplexing, while maintaining the computing accuracy and energy efficiency. • We evaluate AIR-LLM on Sionna ray-tracing and real RF mixer profiling, showing its near-lossless PPL on LLM tasks with orders-of-magnitude less energy and airtime. 2. Analog GEMV via RF Mixers An RF mixer is a fundamental component on edge devices for up/down conversion. Essentially, it performs analog multiplication in the time domain, corresponding to the linear convolution in the frequency domain, where OFDM signals reside. Such a convolution operation can be leveraged for GEMV in ML inference. Complex-valued linear convolution. The complex-valued nature of wireless signals allows an RF mixer to perform, in analog, the complex-valued linear convolution (denoted by ∗\ast) between two input signals of equal subcarrier spacing Δ​f\Delta f. To simplify, we assume they have the same FFT size (NfftN_{\textrm{fft}}) so that we denote the frequency-domain input activation signal by X∈ℂNfftX\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\textrm{fft}}}, and the weight signal by W∈ℂNfftW\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\textrm{fft}}}. This process yields the output activation signal Y∈ℂ2​Nfft−1Y\in\mathbb{C}^{2N_{\textrm{fft}}-1} as (3) Y⁡[k]=(W∗X)​[k]=∑k′W⁡[k′]⋅X⁡[k−k′].\displaystyle Y[k]=\left(W\ast X\right)[k]=\sum_{k^{\prime}}W[k^{\prime}]\cdot X[k-k^{\prime}]. Leveraging linear convolution for GEMVs/IPs. We examine the real-valued GEMV that ML inference is built upon, formulated by 𝐘=𝐖⋅𝐗\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{W}\cdot\mathbf{X} with 𝐖∈ℝM×N\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}, 𝐗∈ℝN\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}, and 𝐘∈ℝM\mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{M}. This GEMV can be broken down into MM independent NN-element inner products (IPs), each of which takes 2​N−12N-1 FLOPs. Since the linear convolution in (3) is complex-valued whereas the GEMV is real-valued, a single pair of input and weight signals carries two such IPs. Substituting (4) into (3), the middle subcarrier of the output signal, Y⁡[N−1]Y[N-1], is exactly the one that accumulates all the NN element-wise products, i.e., Ym,m′​[N−1]\displaystyle Y_{m,m^{\prime}}[N-1] =∑k=0N−1(𝐖⁡[m,k]+j⋅𝐖⁡[m′,k])⋅𝐗⁡[k]\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\left(\mathbf{W}[m,k]+{j}\cdot\mathbf{W}[m^{\prime},k]\right)\cdot\mathbf{X}[k] (5) =𝐘⁡[m]+j⋅𝐘⁡[m′],\displaystyle=\mathbf{Y}[m]+{j}\cdot\mathbf{Y}[m^{\prime}], so that the two IPs are read off the real and the imaginary parts of this same subcarrier without interfering with each other, while the remaining 2​N−22N-2 subcarriers are discarded. RF Computing Engine In this section, we present the RF computing engine of AIR-LLM on the edge device based on MIMO, as shown in Fig. 2, where AIR-LLM calibrates the channel of the broadcast weights with a pair of precoder and postcoder that are compatible with the RF mixer-driven analog GEMV. Figure 2. The overview of AIR-LLM’s RF computing engine, which completes AA IPs of the GEMV per round (or 2​A2A if real-valued). The central radio broadcasts the weights of these IPs over its AA antennas, without user-specific precoding. Each edge user then feeds the AA received weight waveforms, together with its own GEMV input, into CC calibration units, whose precoders and postcoders are derived from that user’s own channel by an SVD-based initialization and an ALS-based fine-tuning. Summing the outputs of the CC units gives the GEMV output of this round. 3.1. System Efficiency Analysis We analyze the efficiency of AIR-LLM along two dimensions: the airtime it occupies the wireless channel, and the energy it consumes on the edge device. Airtime analysis. The airtime of AIR-LLM is inversely proportional to the number of antennas AA and the occupied bandwidth BB. Interestingly, this form exactly follows a conventional communication link with spatial multiplexing on AA and frequency multiplexing on BB. On the other hand, AIR-LLM’s airtime is independent of the SNR, which instead determines the computing accuracy; AIR-LLM therefore does not customize the transmitted signals for each user, and is naturally fit to broadcasting. Leveraged by broadcasting, one transmission of the weights serves arbitrarily many edge users at a constant airtime, so the airtime amortized per user decreases as 1/U1/U. The complete analysis is given in Appendix C.3. Energy analysis. Overall, AIR-LLM achieves good energy efficiency on RF computing, whose energy per FLOP is further averaged down as the GEMV scales up to LLM. This is because the energy consumption of almost every hardware component in AIR-LLM is amortized by either the input size NN or the output size MM, leaving the DAC, whose per-FLOP energy is set by the antenna number AA and the unit number CC, as the floor that a large GEMV converges to. Such a scaling law is contributed by two key designs. First, the RF mixer and the LPF collapse the whole input dimension into a single subcarrier with a downsampling ratio of NN, so the ADC takes only one sample per inner product, which usually dominates the energy budget of an analog computing system; the postcoding runs on that same single sample per antenna, so its energy is amortized by NN as well. Second, the precoding and the IFFT are paid only once per GEMV, as the same precoded input signal 𝐱′\mathbf{x}^{\prime} is reused across all the ⌈M/(2​A)⌉\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil rounds, so their energy is amortized by the output size MM. The per-component analysis is in Appendix C.4. Tradeoff on computing accuracy, airtime, and energy. The calibration unit number CC is where these three metrics meet. On the accuracy side, OPT-Chan calibrates the channel with a rank-CC approximation, so a larger CC leaves a smaller residual and thus a more accurate channel calibration; and the more antennas AA are deployed, the larger CC this accuracy requires. On the energy side, however, every energy term grows linearly with CC. Scaling up AA therefore shortens the airtime but pays for its accuracy in energy, so CC should be the smallest that meets the target task’s accuracy. 4. Implementation We implement AIR-LLM on the wireless channels of real-world urban scenes by a ray-tracing simulator, and on the distortion of a real RF mixer, measured on a wired testbed. 4.1. Channel Modeling by Ray Tracing (a) Paris (b) Munich (c) Testbed Figure 4. The two Sionna ray-tracing scenes in Paris (a) and Munich (b), and the testbed for RF mixer profiling. Sionna ray-tracing simulator. We build the wireless channel between the central radio and the edge devices on top of NVIDIA Sionna’s ray-tracing engine (v2.0.1) (Hoydis et al., 2022; Hoydis et al., 2023). Specifically, Sionna simulates the wireless signal propagation process by shooting 10710^{7} rays into a digital twin of a real-world city scene and resolving their interactions (e.g., reflection, refraction, and diffraction) with the buildings, grounds, etc. Assembling these propagation paths, it provides the realistic channel HH that the weight signal 𝐖\mathbf{W} propagates through to each of the edge devices. As shown in Fig. 4(a) and (b), we evaluate AIR-LLM in two contrasting urban scenes: (i) Place Charles de Gaulle in Paris, open enough that a line-of-sight (LOS) path always holds, and (ii) the city center of Munich, densely built so that multipath is rich while the LOS path is often blocked. Central radio configuration. The central radio sits at the center of each scene, 10 m above the ground. It carries AA antennas (A=4A=4 by default) on ⌈A/2⌉\left\lceil{A/2}\right\rceil physical elements, each of two orthogonal polarizations, spaced 1.7 m apart. It broadcasts the weight signal on the CBRS band (Sohul et al., 2015) at a 3.5 GHz carrier frequency over 100 MHz of bandwidth. The default broadcast power per antenna is set to 50 dBm, and the coverage radius is 100 m. Edge device configuration. We randomly drop 100 edge devices at 1.5 m height within the central radio’s coverage zone. Each edge device carries the same cross-polarized AA-port array with 4.3 cm spacing (half-wavelength), and C=8C=8 calibration units, whose coders are derived from a least-squares per-antenna pilot estimate H^\widehat{H}. We assume the devices’ noise figure of 4 dB, corresponding to a noise floor of -90 dBm across the 100 MHz bandwidth; their path loss (PL) from the central radio is estimated by its own channel as −10​log10⁡(𝔼⁡[|H|2])-10\log_{10}(\mathbb{E}[|H|^{2}]). 4.2. Hardware Profiling on Real RF Mixer RF mixers are not built for analog multiplication, and hence distort the desired product. We therefore measure the distortion of a real RF mixer, ZEM-4300+ (Mini-Circuits, 2024), driven by USRP X310 radios (Ettus Research, 2024) as the transceivers, as shown in Fig. 4(c). The profiling is wired, so the power entering the mixer stays far above the noise floor; the link is thus considered noiseless, and the computing errors are fully attributed to the mixer’s own distortion. Specifically, for each power at the mixer’s RF port, which receives the weight signal over the air in a deployment, we sweep the power at its LO port and keep the lowest distortion error, i.e., the best effective number of bits (ENOB), that the mixer reaches. The measured distortion ENOB curve over the RF power is shown in Fig. A2 of Appendix E.1. In our evaluation, we read this curve at each edge device’s received weight signal power and plug in the corresponding distortion error. 5. Evaluation 5.1. In applications whose GEMV input is itself an analog waveform, e.g., a received wireless signal or a biomedical sensor readout, this bottlenecked DAC energy is waived as well. This is exactly the regime an LLM runs in, whose inference is dominated by large GEMVs, and where AIR-LLM therefore costs the edge device the least. 5.2. Serving an LLM is memory-bounded by the weight movement rather than arithmetic (Guo et al., 2025). One category of works shrinks the bits per weight and co-designs the compute units around the resulting mixed-format GEMVs (Frantar et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2023; Tseng et al., 2024), with the hardware absorbing the outliers (Guo et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024) or the dequantization (Park et al., 2025; Mo et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026); a second attacks the movement rather than the format, placing the compute next to the memory that holds the weights and the KV cache (Park et al., 2024; Heo et al., 2024; Yun et al., 2024). All share one premise: the weights are already stored in the device’s memory, and only the cost of fetching and multiplying a resident weight is optimized. AIR-LLM removes that premise: no weight is stored on the edge device; each arrival of the broadcast weight waveform is consumed and computed directly in the RF/analog domain. Analog computing for ML inference. Analog computing performs the FLOPs in physics rather than in digital, escaping the energy floor of digital arithmetic: in-memory computing completes a GEMV on a ReRAM, PCM, or SRAM crossbar through Ohm’s and Kirchhoff’s laws (Shafiee et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2022; Le Gallo et al., 2023), while photonic computing multiplies operands encoded onto light (Shen et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2023). However, such designs are usually limited by their analog error and readout converters (Zhang et al., 2025; Khaddam-Aljameh et al., 2022), yet already carry real models at a handful of effective bits (Ambrogio et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024); AIR-LLM likewise reports every result at the effective bits its link resolves (Dettmers and Zettlemoyer, 2023). Closest in spirit is the work that lets operand delivery and computation happen in the same physical layer, over fiber (Sludds et al., 2022) or over the air (Reus-Muns et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2026b; Gao et al., 2026a), the latter inside a commodity receiver’s RF mixer; unlike over-the-air computation, which superposes many transmitters into a sum (Nazer and Gastpar, 2007; Zhu et al., 2020), AIR-LLM’s mixer forms a product of an arriving weight waveform with a local input. In addition, AIR-LLM generalizes the single-antenna and single-weight-stream into an A×AA\times A MIMO engine to largely reduce the airtime, whose calibration units zero-force a real, frequency-selective channel. LLM deployment on the edge. On-device LLM serving is a capacity problem before a compute one, and the systems response keeps as few weights resident as possible: pruning (Niu et al., 2020), activation sparsity (Song et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024), flash streaming (Alizadeh et al., 2024), or accelerator–model co-design (Yu et al., 2024). Yet even a quantized resident model stays memory-bound on commodity phones, where energy and thermals make continuous generation untenable (Laskaridis et al., 2024). The complementary response moves the model off the device (Kwon et al., 2023; Stojkovic et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2017), trading the memory wall for a per-query network cost and for handing the prompt to the server. Both leave each device paying, privately and per token, for the same weights that every other device in the cell also pays for (Qu et al., 2024). AIR-LLM instead disaggregates the weight storage to the central radio while keeping both the computation and the prompt on the edge, and because its transmission is edge-device-unaware, one broadcast is mixed by every device in the coverage at once, amortizing the delivery cost over the devices served. Such one-to-many analog delivery has precedent in SoftCast (Jakubczak and Katabi, 2011), which broadcasts video over raw OFDM at a fidelity set by each receiver’s own channel. 7. Conclusion In this paper, we present AIR-LLM, an LLM inference architecture for edge users that is memory-access-free, user-scalable and energy-efficient. Specifically, AIR-LLM exploits MIMO spatial multiplexing to deliver multiple weight streams at a time and thereby shorten the airtime, and the design of the precoder–postcoder pair on the edge user energy-efficiently calibrates its own wireless channel. Exhaustive evaluations on the NVIDIA Sionna ray-traced channels and the profiling of a real RF mixer reveal that, with a slight PPL gap to the FP16 baseline, AIR-LLM cuts the per-token energy and airtime by orders of magnitude. We believe AIR-LLM opens up a new path for the next generation of edge intelligence. Acknowledgements. Appendix B Blocked Correlation Operation We generalize the linear-convolution mapping into a blocked correlation operation (BCO), where the mixer retains a whole output block of subcarriers rather than a single one. B.1. Definition and Realization Definition of BCO. We define the BCO by ⋆\star. Its two operands, weights and inputs, are both complex valued, given by 𝐰∈ℂD×Lw\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{C}^{D\times L_{w}} and 𝐱∈ℂD×Lx\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{D\times L_{x}}, each consisting of DD blocks. These DD blocks are correlated in parallel, and their correlation outputs are accumulated into a single output block 𝐲∈ℂL\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{C}^{L}, defined as 𝐲⁡[k]\displaystyle\mathbf{y}[k] =(𝐰⋆𝐱)​[k]\displaystyle=\left(\mathbf{w}\star\mathbf{x}\right)[k] (14) =∑d=0D−1∑k′=max⁡(0,k−Lx+1)min⁡(k,Lw−1)𝐰⁡[d,k′]⋅𝐱⁡[d,k′−k+Lx−1],\displaystyle=\sum_{d=0}^{D-1}\sum_{k^{\prime}=\max(0,\,k-L_{x}+1)}^{\min(k,\,L_{w}-1)}\mathbf{w}[d,k^{\prime}]\cdot\mathbf{x}[d,k^{\prime}-k+L_{x}-1], where the block sizes satisfy L=Lw+Lx−1L=L_{w}+L_{x}-1. A BCO thus costs D​Lw​LxDL_{w}L_{x} additions and as many multiplications, i.e., 2​D​Lw​Lx2DL_{w}L_{x} FLOPs. Realizing BCO with an RF mixer. In the frequency domain, an RF mixer convolves two analog signals, WW and XX, into YY, which is the correlation of (14) once one operand is reversed in subcarrier order, as in (4). To realize a BCO, we let the FFT size be Nfft=D⋅LN_{\textrm{fft}}=D\cdot L, i.e., one length-LL subcarrier slot per block. The frequency-domain weight signal W∈ℂD​LW\in\mathbb{C}^{DL} is obtained from 𝐰\mathbf{w} by zero-padding each block 𝐰[d,:]\mathbf{w}[d,:] into the length-LL segment W[dL:(d+1)L−1]W[dL:(d+1)L-1], and the input signal X∈ℂD​LX\in\mathbb{C}^{DL} is obtained from 𝐱\mathbf{x} in the same way, i.e., (15) W⁡[d​L+k]\displaystyle W[dL+k] ={𝐰⁡[d,k],k<Lw,0,k≥Lw,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathbf{w}[d,k],&k<L_{w},\\ 0,&k\geq L_{w},\end{cases} X⁡[d​L+k]\displaystyle X[dL+k] ={𝐱⁡[d,k],k<Lx,0,k≥Lx,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathbf{x}[d,k],&k<L_{x},\\ 0,&k\geq L_{x},\end{cases} for all d=0,1,…,D−1d=0,1,\dots,D-1 and k=0,1,…,L−1k=0,1,\dots,L-1. The zero padding guarantees that the correlation of one block never leaks into the subcarrier slot of the next. Correlating WW with XX spans 2​D−12D-1 slots, and every matching block pair (d,d)(d,d) lands in the same, middle slot of index D−1D-1, which therefore accumulates the correlation outputs of all DD blocks, exactly as (14) prescribes. This middle slot is extracted by the LPF, whose output signal Y∈ℂLY\in\mathbb{C}^{L} satisfies Y⁡[k]=𝐲⁡[k]Y[k]=\mathbf{y}[k] for all k=0,1,…,L−1k=0,1,\dots,L-1. Since the subcarrier spacing Δ​f\Delta f is shared by all three signals, this output occupies a bandwidth of only B/DB/D and is digitized with D×D\times fewer ADC samples than the full-band signal, which is where AIR-LLM’s ADC energy saving comes from. Implication on the calibration units. The calibration unit of §3.3 carries over unchanged, with one structural caveat on the precoder. Under BCO, the LL subcarriers within a block jointly carry one correlation, so they must be scaled identically: a per-subcarrier precoder would reweight the individual correlation taps and destroy the block structure of (14). The precoder is therefore constant within each block, i.e., Ppre∈ℂC×DP_{\textrm{pre}}\in\mathbb{C}^{C\times D} with the subcarrier kk driven by Ppre​[c,⌊k/L⌋]P_{\textrm{pre}}[c,\left\lfloor{k/L}\right\rfloor], which is precisely the form optimized in (17) of §B.2. The postcoder, in contrast, acts across antennas only and is applied identically to all subcarriers, so it is unaffected. For a GEMV, L=1L=1 makes the per-block and the per-subcarrier precoder identical, recovering the main-body design. B.2. Convergence of the Optimization We study how the two-step solve converges on the GEMV, i.e., the degenerate case L=1L=1 in which (17) reduces to the OPT-Chan of §3.3. The two edge devices are the selected users of Paris and Munich of §5.1, resolving approximately 4.00 and 3.00 bit, so the numbers below are directly comparable to the evaluation. What each step buys. Fig. A1 traces the two steps on the selected edge device of each scene. Before either of them, the raw link is unusable: fitting the single complex gain that an AGC and a carrier recovery already provide leaves 0.00 bit in Paris and 0.05 bit in Munich, i.e., the frequency selectivity of HH and its inter-antenna mixing alone destroy the GEMV. The closed-form Step-1 initialization recovers most of it at once, cutting the loss of (17) from 0.998 to 0.013 in Paris and from 0.947 to 0.259 in Munich, i.e., to 3.12 and 0.97 bit. The gap between the two scenes is the price of the per-block channel approximation of (19): the richer multipath of Munich makes the frequency response vary within a block, so the averaged H¯\bar{H} that Step 1 inverts sits further from the per-subcarrier channel that (17) actually scores, and the SVD initialization alone is worth about one bit there against three in Paris. How many ALS iterations. Figs. A1 and A1 answer how long Step 2 has to run. A single ALS pass recovers most of what Step 1 leaves behind, dropping the loss by a further 2.7×\times in Paris and 17.5×\times in Munich to reach 3.79 and 2.85 bit. Since one iteration is two closed-form least-squares solves and the optimization runs once per channel coherence time rather than per GEMV, we run it to that convergence throughout the evaluation, though stopping after the first pass would already sit within 0.29 bit of it. Appendix C Airtime and Energy Consumption This section analyzes the two efficiency metrics of AIR-LLM, the airtime and the energy consumption per FLOP. We derive them at the general block size of a BCO (§C.1 and §C.2), and then substitute the GEMV mapping of the main body, its degenerate case, to read off the airtime and the energy of a GEMV (§C.3 and §C.4). C.1. Airtime of a BCO We analyze the airtime of AIR-LLM, i.e., how long the RF chain of an edge device is occupied to compute one FLOP. It is bottlenecked by the duration of the signals, both the wireless one carrying 𝐖\mathbf{W} from the central radio and the local one carrying 𝐱\mathbf{x}, which the bandwidth BB sets. Airtime per round. Each round of AIR-LLM receives one OFDM symbol carrying 𝐖\mathbf{W} across the Nfft=D​LN_{\textrm{fft}}=DL subcarriers, feeding AA antennas/RF mixers for 2​A2A parallel BCOs, two of them packed per antenna into the real and the imaginary parts; a layer of MM outputs, all sharing the same input 𝐱\mathbf{x}, thus takes ⌈M/(2​A)⌉\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil rounds. The airtime per round then scales as (23) T∝D​LB.\displaystyle T\propto\frac{DL}{B}. Airtime per FLOP. Normalizing (23) by the FLOPs that the 2​A2A parallel BCOs complete within the round gives the per-FLOP airtime of a general BCO, (24) τ∝LA​B​Lw​Lx.\displaystyle\tau\propto\frac{L}{ABL_{w}L_{x}}. The block number DD cancels out: splitting a layer into more, smaller blocks lengthens the round and adds FLOPs in the same proportion. More generally, (24) rewards a block layout whose output block is short relative to the product of the two input block sizes, i.e., one whose correlation reuses each transmitted weight over many taps. C.2. Energy Consumption of a BCO We analyze the edge-device-side energy consumption of AIR-LLM per FLOP by its complexity, i.e., the number of operations on three kinds of hardware, each costing a constant energy per operation: the DAC and the ADC, counted in samples, and the digital computing, counted in FLOPs. Energy per module. We account for the energy of one whole module, i.e., all ⌈M/(2​A)⌉\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil rounds of 2​A2A BCOs, and then normalize by the FLOPs it completes, breaking the module energy into seven components along the signal chain, (25) E=Epre+Eifft+Edac+Eadc+Efft+Epost+Esum,\displaystyle E=E_{\textrm{pre}}+E_{\textrm{ifft}}+E_{\textrm{dac}}+E_{\textrm{adc}}+E_{\textrm{fft}}+E_{\textrm{post}}+E_{\textrm{sum}}, i.e., the precoding, the IFFT, the DAC, the ADC, the FFT, the postcoding, and the cross-unit summation. Each of the CC calibration units precodes 𝐱\mathbf{x} per block and takes an NfftN_{\textrm{fft}}-point IFFT. Both are paid only once for the whole module: PpreP_{\textrm{pre}} depends solely on the channel and every round mixes the same 𝐱\mathbf{x} with a new set of broadcast weights, so the precoded waveform is buffered and replayed across the rounds. Within each of the ⌈M/(2​A)⌉≈M/(2​A)\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil\approx M/(2A) rounds, every unit then converts the waveform with one DAC over Nfft=D​LN_{\textrm{fft}}=DL samples, digitizes the LPF output of LL samples per antenna, and decodes it with a LL-point FFT plus postcoding, before the CC units are summed. Accumulating the latter five over the rounds gives the “Energy per module” column of Tab. A3, and dividing each term by the 2​M​D​Lw​Lx2MDL_{w}L_{x} FLOPs of the module gives its “Energy per FLOP” column. Note that the ADC term is charged for LL samples rather than NfftN_{\textrm{fft}}, since the BCO output occupies only the reduced bandwidth B/DB/D. Table A3. The energy complexity of one module on AIR-LLM under BCO and the seven terms per FLOP. Unlike the airtime of (24), the block number DD does not cancel here: it amortizes the receiver-side terms while it stretches the IFFT logarithmically, which is the trade-off a concrete block layout has to settle. C.3. Airtime of a GEMV Airtime per GEMV. Under the GEMV mapping, D=ND=N and Lw=Lx=L=1L_{w}=L_{x}=L=1, so that Nfft=NN_{\textrm{fft}}=N and each round of (23) produces 2​A2A IPs. A GEMV of MM IPs therefore takes ⌈M/(2​A)⌉\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil such rounds in serial, i.e., a signal duration per GEMV of (26) T∝M​NA​B.\displaystyle T\propto\frac{MN}{AB}. Airtime per FLOP. Within this duration, AIR-LLM completes the entire GEMV of M⁡(2​N−1)M(2N-1) FLOPs, so that (27) τ∝1A​B,\displaystyle\tau\propto\frac{1}{AB}, which is (24) at unit block sizes. Airtime scaling law. Notably, both layer sizes NN and MM cancel out of (27): a larger GEMV proportionally stretches the signal duration and the number of FLOPs completed within it, leaving the per-FLOP airtime unchanged. What remains is governed solely by the bandwidth BB and the antenna number AA, independent of the SNR. C.4. Energy Consumption of a GEMV Table A4. The energy complexity of one GEMV on AIR-LLM and the same seven terms per FLOP, along the signal chain. Reading the seven terms at unit block sizes. Substituting D=ND=N and Lw=Lx=L=1L_{w}=L_{x}=L=1 into the “Energy per module” column of Tab. A3 gives the “Energy per GEMV” column of Tab. A4, and dividing by the 2​M​N2MN FLOPs of the GEMV gives its “Energy per FLOP” column. Two terms are worth reading out at these block sizes. The ADC is charged for a single sample: the RF-mixer output has been low-pass filtered into a single-subcarrier bandwidth of Δ​f\Delta f, so one complex sample captures the outputs of the whole IP pair by its real and imaginary components. The FFT term vanishes with log2⁡L\log_{2}L, as the FFT that follows the ADC is trivial for its single sample per antenna. Energy consumption scaling law. Summing the six remaining per-FLOP terms of Tab. A4 gives the energy per FLOP of AIR-LLM. Every term of this per-FLOP energy consumption is amortized by one of the dimensions as the GEMV scales up in LLM: • Amortization over the input size NN: the ADC, postcoding, and summation terms scale as 1/N1/N, as one ADC sample squeezes the whole input dimension into a scalar, on which the postcoding and the summation are performed regardless of NN. • Amortization over the output size MM: the precoding and IFFT terms scale as 1/M1/M, as the precoded waveform is stored and reused across all the rounds of a GEMV. • Amortization over the antenna number AA: the DAC term scales as 1/A1/A, as its single waveform is fanned out to all the AA RF mixers. Among the three, the DAC term is the bottleneck, since A≪N,MA\ll N,M in practice: it is amortized only by how many antennas an edge device can physically deploy, which massive MIMO keeps relieving as it scales up the array. Appendix D AIR-LLM in CNN Convolutional (CONV) layers, which dominate CNNs, do not fit the one-subcarrier-per-output mapping of the main body: reusing the same kernel across all I2I^{2} positions of an image would require re-transmitting that kernel once per output pixel, so the broadcast weight traffic, the very resource AIR-LLM is built to save, would grow by I2I^{2}. The BCO of Appendix B removes that restriction, as one mixing round now retains a whole output block instead of a single subcarrier, and a kernel broadcast once is correlated against every position of the image within it. We map a Conv2D layer onto the BCO (§D.1), and then specialize the BCO airtime of §C.1 and the BCO energy of §C.2 to it (§D.2 and §D.3). D.1. Mapping Conv2D onto BCO Layer formulation. We examine a general Conv2D layer with a kernel size of K×KK\times K, an image size of I×II\times I, NN input channels, and MM output channels, so that 𝐖(CONV)∈ℝN×M×K×K\mathbf{W}^{\textrm{(CONV)}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M\times K\times K}, 𝐗(CONV)∈ℝN×I×I\mathbf{X}^{\textrm{(CONV)}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times I\times I}, and 𝐘(CONV)∈ℝM×I×I\mathbf{Y}^{\textrm{(CONV)}}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times I\times I}. We assume KK is odd and that the correlation is zero-padded to preserve the image size. Just as a GEMV decomposes into MM inner products, this Conv2D decomposes into MM independent sub-convolutions, one per output channel, each of which becomes one BCO; as the layer is real-valued whereas the BCO is complex-valued, two output channels are packed into the real and the imaginary parts of a single BCO, as the two IPs of (4) are. Blocks as input channels, subcarriers as pixels. For each sub-convolution we set D=ND=N, letting one block correspond to one input channel, so that the block accumulation in (14) performs exactly the summation over input channels. To embed the 2D image correlation into the 1D BCO, we flatten the I×II\times I image row by row and pad each row with KK zeros, so that the correlation of one row does not leak into the next; this gives each row a slot of length I+KI+K, hence (28) Lx=I⁡(I+K).\displaystyle L_{x}=I(I+K). The kernel is flattened the same way, row by row, but each of its rows is instead padded with II zeros so that its row stride matches that of the flattened image, giving (29) Lw=K⁡(I+K).\displaystyle L_{w}=K(I+K). Following L=Lw+Lx−1L=L_{w}+L_{x}-1 and approximating away the −1-1, the output block length is (30) L≈(I+K)2,\displaystyle L\approx(I+K)^{2}, out of which the I2I^{2} subcarriers sitting at the valid correlation lags carry 𝐘(CONV)\mathbf{Y}^{\textrm{(CONV)}} of this output channel, and the remainder are discarded together with the LPF-rejected slots. Repeating this over all MM output channels sweeps 𝐰m\mathbf{w}_{m} and 𝐲m\mathbf{y}_{m} while sharing the same 𝐱\mathbf{x}, exactly the structure the central radio broadcasts and the AA antennas consume in parallel, two output channels per antenna. Notably, the kernel is broadcast once for the whole image: the reuse of a kernel across positions is absorbed by the correlation itself rather than paid for in weight traffic. Padding overhead. The MM BCOs nominally complete 2​N​M​K​I​(I+K)22NMKI(I+K)^{2} FLOPs, of which only 2​N​M​K2​I22NMK^{2}I^{2} are useful to the CONV layer; the rest are correlation taps created by the zero padding. We denote this inefficiency by the ratio of nominal to useful FLOPs, (31) η=(I+K)2K​I≥1,\displaystyle\eta=\frac{(I+K)^{2}}{KI}\geq 1, which approaches I/KI/K for I≫KI\gg K. All per-FLOP metrics below are reported per useful FLOP, i.e., scaled by η\eta, so that they are directly comparable with the GEMV results of the main body. D.2. Airtime of Conv2D Airtime per FLOP. Substituting (28)–(30) into the per-FLOP airtime of a general BCO in (24), and scaling by the padding overhead η\eta of (31), yields the airtime per useful FLOP of a Conv2D layer, (32) τCONV∝η⋅LA​B​Lw​Lx=1A​B⋅(I+K)2K2​I2.\displaystyle\tau_{\textrm{CONV}}\propto\eta\cdot\frac{L}{ABL_{w}L_{x}}=\frac{1}{AB}\cdot\frac{(I+K)^{2}}{K^{2}I^{2}}. Comparison against GEMV. Against the GEMV airtime τGEMV\tau_{\textrm{GEMV}} of (27), which shares the same proportionality constant, we have (33) τCONVτGEMV=(I+K)2K2​I2→I≫K1K2.\displaystyle\frac{\tau_{\textrm{CONV}}}{\tau_{\textrm{GEMV}}}=\frac{(I+K)^{2}}{K^{2}I^{2}}\xrightarrow{~I\gg K~}\frac{1}{K^{2}}. Interestingly, despite the padding inefficiency η\eta, a Conv2D layer is faster per useful FLOP than a GEMV, occupying up to K2×K^{2}\times less airtime. This is because the BCO’s block-wise correlation structure is intrinsically matched to the convolution’s reuse of one kernel across all positions of the image: a single OFDM symbol that carries K2K^{2} kernel taps produces I2I^{2} output pixels, whereas under the GEMV mapping the same symbol duration would produce only one. Assuming I≫KI\gg K, so that Lx≈L≈I2L_{x}\approx L\approx I^{2} and Lw≈K​IL_{w}\approx KI in (28)–(30), and substituting the Conv2D mapping (D=ND=N) into the “Energy per module” column of Tab. A3 gives that of Tab. A5, and dividing by the 2​N​M​K2​I22NMK^{2}I^{2} useful FLOPs of the layer gives its “Energy per useful FLOP” column. Takeaways. Two opposite trends are visible in Tab. A5. On the one hand, the ADC and the cross-unit-summation terms both carry 1/N1/N and vanish as the layer deepens, exactly as in the GEMV case of Tab. A4: one ADC sample and one cross-unit addition now serve an entire input channel of the image rather than a single weight element, which is the saving that the reduced output bandwidth B/DB/D buys and that the remote baseline cannot obtain. The DAC term likewise decays as 1/K21/K^{2}, mirroring the airtime gain of (33). On the other hand, the digital encoding and decoding terms do not cancel as cleanly. Each of them does carry an amortization of its own, the transmitter-side precoding and IFFT over MM and the receiver-side FFT and postcoding over NN, so all three dimensions of §C.4 survive the Conv2D mapping intact. What survives with them, however, is a logarithmic factor the GEMV mapping does not have: the IFFT over all N​I2NI^{2} subcarriers and the receive FFT over the I2I^{2} subcarriers of a block leave a residual log2⁡(N​I)\log_{2}(NI) and log2⁡I\log_{2}I that both grow with the image size. Consequently, unlike the airtime of §D.2, where a larger kernel or image is strictly beneficial, the energy of Conv2D trades the analog savings on the converters against the digital cost of the wider OFDM symbol, and the two must be weighed together when choosing AIR-LLM’s operating point. Fig. A2 reports the wired sweep of §4: at each power delivered to the mixer’s RF port, the LO power is swept and the best ENOB is kept. The ENOB climbs with the RF power and then flattens as the mixer’s own nonlinearity takes over from the drive level; this knee is the distortion floor that the saturated users of §5.3 sit on. Path loss across the candidate devices. Fig. A3 shows the PL distribution of the 100 candidate devices dropped in each scene, from which the representative devices of §5.1 are selected. The open scene of Paris is tightly concentrated, a single mode of median 84.0 dB with 5/95-th percentiles of 74.9/97.8 dB, since almost every drop keeps an LOS path to the central radio. The dense scene of Munich is both worse and far wider, a median of 91.4 dB and percentiles of 75.2/131.3 dB, with a long shadowed tail of devices whose LOS path is blocked by a building. Both scenes therefore span the range of link qualities from the noise-limited users of §5.3 to the distortion-limited ones. E.2. Baselines We benchmark AIR-LLM against digital baselines along two dimensions: the precision at which the weights are kept, and the weight storage from which they reach the edge device. Precision dimension. We take FP16 as the exact reference, and further consider weight-only quantization (WoQ) at 4/3 bit, i.e., W4A16 and W3A16, by RTN, GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023), and AWQ (Lin et al., 2024). Analog computing baselines. We further benchmark against two analog computing baselines at the same ENOB as AIR-LLM’s device: (i) AWGN, additive Gaussian noise on each GEMV output, and (ii) HyFlexPIM, a multiplicative Gaussian error on each weight, i.e., the conductance spread of a memristive crossbar. The former error is redrawn per GEMV, whereas the latter is frozen on the weights; AIR-LLM sits in between, as its thermal noise is redrawn per transmission while its calibration residual and mixer distortion hold for as long as the channel does. Weight storage dimension. Under remote storage, the weights are kept on the central radio and delivered to the edge device over the same wireless channel as AIR-LLM’s by a standard communication link. Under local storage, they are instead pre-stored in the edge device’s memory. AIR-LLM targets the remote storage, which is both more realistic for edge computing and more challenging than the local one. E.3. Evaluation Tasks and Metrics Benchmarking GEMV with ENOB. We first benchmark AIR-LLM on a single GEMV 𝐲=𝐖⋅𝐱\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{W}\cdot\mathbf{x}, whose weights 𝐖\mathbf{W} and inputs 𝐱\mathbf{x} are randomly drawn from i.i.d. Gaussian distributions, and quantify its computing accuracy by the effective number of bits (ENOB), defined as (34) ENOB=−12⋅log2(𝔼𝐱,𝐖[1M∑m=0M−1|𝐲m−𝐲^m|2]),\displaystyle\textsf{ENOB}=-\frac{1}{2}\cdot\log_{2}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{W}}\left[\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}\left|\mathbf{y}_{m}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{m}\right|^{2}\right]\right), where both the ground truth 𝐲\mathbf{y} and its estimate 𝐲^\hat{\mathbf{y}} are normalized by the standard deviation of 𝐲\mathbf{y}. A trivial estimate 𝐲^=𝟎\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{0} thus sits at exactly 0 bit. PPL and zero-shot accuracy on LLM. We then run whole LLMs over AIR-LLM, including LLaMA-3.2 (1B and 3B) (Meta AI, 2024), LLaMA-3.1 (8B and 70B) (Grattafiori et al., 2024), LLaMA-2 (7B and 13B) (Touvron et al., 2023), Mistral-7B (Jiang et al., 2023), and Gemma-4 (E2B and E4B) (Gemma Team, 2026), where every weight-activation GEMV is performed by AIR-LLM’s RF computing and the rest stays digital. We report (i) the PPL on WikiText-2 (Merity et al., 2017) and (ii) the zero-shot accuracy on PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), ARC-e and ARC-c (Clark et al., 2018), BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), and WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2020). Airtime and energy consumption. We further report the airtime and the energy consumption per token. The airtime is the time one token occupies the wireless link, the resource the central radio rations across the edge devices it serves; for the remote storage baselines, it is counted on the same ray-traced channel under a standard-compliant 5G NR link (3GPP, 2022a; 3GPP, 2022b), while the local storage baselines occupy no airtime. The energy consumption is based on the per-operation energies of state-of-the-art DACs (Olieman et al., 2015), ADCs (Harpe et al., 2011; Murmann, 2026), digital computing (NVIDIA, 2024), and data movement (Antepara et al., 2025). This metric is harsher on analog computing than the PPL, because of how it is scored: every candidate continuation is concatenated to the same stem and run through its own inference pass, and the answer is the candidate with the highest log-likelihood. An error that is deterministic given the weights, the quantization grid of WoQ or the frozen conductance spread of HyFlexPIM, shifts all the candidates of a question in the same direction, so the comparison among them, and thus the argmax, largely survives. A non-deterministic one does not: the AWGN baseline and AIR-LLM’s thermal noise are redrawn independently in every pass, so each candidate is scored under its own realization of the error, and the choice flips whenever that perturbation exceeds the log-likelihood margin between the candidates. The central radio may send the same weight signal several times and let the edge device average the copies, which trades airtime for a lower thermal noise: repeating it nn times costs nn times the airtime and lowers the noise power by 10​log10​n10\log_{10}n dB, while leaving the receive chain’s own distortion untouched. The Paris user does not move at all, staying at 6.49 from a single copy to the floor, which confirms the same conclusion as its flat row in Tab. 4: this user is already limited by the channel calibration and the RF mixer rather than by the noise. The noise-limited Munich user does improve, but slowly: 16 copies, i.e., 16 times the airtime, buy 7.37 to 7.19, only 2.4% and already within 0.3% of its 7.17 floor. Repetition is therefore a much worse deal than the transmit power for the same user, which buys 7.9% over the same 10 dB in Tab. 4 at no airtime cost, and we keep a single copy of the weight signal throughout the other evaluations. A10. The channels are re-traced at each carrier with the same scenes, whose ITU-R P.2040 material models are extrapolated below their 1 GHz lower edge for 915 MHz, and the noise floor follows the bandwidth of each band. What the band costs is airtime: its 25 MHz is a quarter of the bandwidth BB that (26) divides, so every GEMV occupies four times the air. At 28 GHz the trade reverses. Paris needs 80 dBm to saturate, 30 dB more than at 3.5 GHz, and saturates 9% worse, at a floor of 7.05 against 6.48; this gap is a distortion floor that no transmit power removes, the sparser multipath of the band leaving each per-subcarrier channel matrix worse conditioned for the calibration units to invert. Its 400 MHz does cut the airtime fourfold, but only for a device close enough to the central radio to spend it. Across the three bands, therefore, the carrier frequency trades airtime against coverage almost one for one, and AIR-LLM is the more comfortable the lower the band, the opposite of where the spectrum for it is easiest to find. blocks.html_en: Abstract.

Next-generation large language models (LLMs) are expanding from the cloud to ubiquitous edge devices. However, edge devices typically either lack the memory to store increasingly large LLM weights or, even with enough memory, spend unaffordable energy on loading the weights. This raises our question: can an edge device run an LLM without storing or loading its weights, but receive them over the air and consume them on the fly? Inspired by wireless broadcasting, we present AIR-LLM, an LLM inference architecture for edge devices, which is composed of: (i) a central radio (e.g., 5G base stations) that broadcasts the LLM weights into the air, and (ii) the edge user that receives the weights and completes the general matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) of LLM inference directly in the radio frequency (RF) domain using RF mixers. To further shorten the airtime, AIR-LLM exploits MIMO spatial multiplexing and proposes an energy-efficient precoder–postcoder pair on the edge to calibrate its own wireless channel. Since the central radio stays user-unaware, AIR-LLM is user-scalable so that one broadcast serves unlimited users within its coverage. We implement AIR-LLM on the NVIDIA Sionna ray-traced channels of two real-world urban scenes and the profiling of a real RF mixer. With a WikiText-2 perplexity degradation of 4.0% on LLaMA-3.1-8B, AIR-LLM saves the energy by 157.7×\times/40.4×\times against the FP16 and weight-only quantization baselines; with 20 users, its airtime is 104.1×\times/26.0×\times shorter, respectively.

blocks.html_en: 1. Introduction

Trillions of edge devices today are embracing emerging machine learning (ML) techniques for a wide range of applications, such as continuous health monitoring (Abbaspourazad et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2025), on-device speech recognition (Radford et al., 2023; Yazdani et al., 2016), and cooperative autonomous driving (Hu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2021). Among these, the emerging large language models (LLMs) provide a unique capability, allowing understanding, reasoning, and generating natural language (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Touvron et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023; Gemma Team, 2026). However, the usage of LLMs on the edge mostly relies on cloud computing, where the locally generated prompts are uploaded to a cloud server, and the responses are downloaded afterwards. This again exposes two typical concerns of cloud computing: the privacy of the sensitive prompts, as well as the round-trip latency, especially when the number of edge users is scaled up (Kang et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2025).

blocks.html_en: The key challenge that hinders such an on-device deployment lies in the daunting model size of today’s LLMs. For example, LLaMA-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) occupies 16 GB in FP16, and still 4 GB after 4-bit weight-only quantization (WoQ) (Frantar et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024). Such a model size stresses an edge device in two stages. First, its memory is typically too small to hold the whole model, so a local deployment has to keep downloading the weights and discarding them afterwards. Second, even if an edge device could store such an LLM entirely, the energy of loading the weights from memory to the computing unit is unaffordable. This is because LLM inference is memory-bounded, especially during the decoding phase, where fetching one weight feeds only two floating-point operations (FLOPs) (Guo et al., 2025). The weight movement therefore dominates the energy, much more than the arithmetic it feeds (Antepara et al., 2025; NVIDIA, 2024).

blocks.html_en: To overcome this, various computing paradigms have been proposed recently. For example, in-memory computing completes the computing in analog within the memory itself, on a ReRAM (Shafiee et al., 2016; Chi et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2022), PCM (Khaddam-Aljameh et al., 2022; Le Gallo et al., 2023), or SRAM (Liu et al., 2026) crossbar, so that the weights are never fetched. Over-the-air computing (Nazer and Gastpar, 2007; Zhu et al., 2020), in turn, superposes the signals of many transmitters over the wireless channel, so that the summation is completed by the channel itself. However, in both cases the size of the general matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) is frozen and limited by the hardware complexity, e.g., a crossbar of 128×\times128 cells (Shafiee et al., 2016) and an array of a few dozen antennas (Reus-Muns et al., 2023). Such a limited GEMV size is naturally incompatible with the LLM whose GEMV sizes keep increasing.

System overview of AIR-LLM: a central radio frequency-encodes the LLM weights onto an OFDM waveform and broadcasts it over the air to serve any edge user within the coverage; the edge user drives the LO with its private activations, and the RF mixer’s output directly carries the GEMV outputs.
The LLM inference is completed once the weight waveform arrives, without ever storing it in memory.
The comparison of AIR-LLM and existing edge computing paradigms.

blocks.html_en: Our motivation lies in the wireless network these edge users already live in. Taking 5G networks as an example, a 5G base station already establishes wireless links to each edge user under its coverage. For these users, accessing the LLM weights is read-only, and thus a purely downlink process; once they run the same LLM, it is exactly what broadcasting was invented for: one transmission simultaneously serving every user in the coverage. Moreover, we employ radio-frequency (RF) computing (Gao et al., 2026b; Gao et al., 2026a), which completes the computing in RF via the passive RF mixer that every receiver already carries. The computing is thereby finished in analog once the broadcast signal arrives, without the weights ever being digitized into the local memory.

blocks.html_en: As shown in Fig. 1, we present AIR-LLM, an LLM inference architecture with (i) a central radio (e.g., a 5G base station) that frequency-encodes the LLM weights onto the subcarriers of an orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) waveform and broadcasts it, and (ii) any edge device in the coverage receives that waveform and computes on it inside its own RF front-end. The key computing component is the RF mixer every wireless device already carries: it multiplies its two inputs in the time domain, corresponding to a linear convolution in the frequency domain. Specifically, driving its local oscillator (LO) with a waveform encoding the activations therefore convolves the arriving weight spectrum with the activation spectrum, and the very middle subcarrier of this convolution is exactly the inner product of the weight and activation vectors. A comparison of existing computing paradigms is presented in Tab. 1.

2.1. OFDM and MIMO Channel Model

OFDM signal structure.   The signals are based on orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM), characterized by the FFT size NfftN_{\textrm{fft}}, i.e., the number of subcarriers in the frequency domain, and the occupied bandwidth BB. The resulting subcarrier spacing is Δ​f=B/Nfft\Delta f=B/N_{\textrm{fft}}.

blocks.html_en: 2.2. Analog GEMV via RF Mixers

An RF mixer is a fundamental component on edge devices for up/down conversion. Essentially, it performs analog multiplication in the time domain, corresponding to the linear convolution in the frequency domain, where OFDM signals reside. Such a convolution operation can be leveraged for GEMV in ML inference.

blocks.html_en: 3. RF Computing Engine

In this section, we present the RF computing engine of AIR-LLM on the edge device based on MIMO, as shown in Fig. 2, where AIR-LLM calibrates the channel of the broadcast weights with a pair of precoder and postcoder that are compatible with the RF mixer-driven analog GEMV.

sentences.en: In this section, we present the RF computing engine of AIR-LLM on the edge device based on MIMO, as shown in Fig. 2, where AIR-LLM calibrates the channel of the broadcast weights with a pair of precoder and postcoder that are compatible with the RF mixer-driven analog GEMV.
The overview of AIR-LLM’s RF computing engine, which completes AA IPs of the GEMV per round (or 2​A2A if real-valued).
The central radio broadcasts the weights of these IPs over its AA antennas, without user-specific precoding.

Each edge user then feeds the AA received weight waveforms, together with its own GEMV input, into CC calibration units, whose precoders and postcoders are derived from that user’s own channel by an SVD-based initialization and an ALS-based fine-tuning.
Summing the outputs of the CC units gives the GEMV output of this round.

blocks.html_en: 3.1. Problem Formulation
We first introduce the basic configuration of the MIMO channel modeling, and then formulate the problem of designing the edge device hardware.

blocks.html_en: GEMV decoupling and IP parallelization.   In AIR-LLM, we consider an A×AA\times A MIMO system for any central radio and edge device pair. This supports up to AA parallel spatial streams, each carrying an IP pair of (4), so that one round of AIR-LLM completes 2​A2A IPs and a GEMV takes ⌈M/(2​A)⌉\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil rounds. blocks.html_en: Channel calibration challenges.   The design of the central radio is edge device-unaware, i.e., does not incorporate any information specific to a particular edge device (e.g., its channel), so that its broadcasting can be generalized for any edge device within its coverage. In this case, the channel effect on 𝐖\mathbf{W} should be entirely calibrated at the edge device side. However, the conventional channel calibration in (2) is not feasible for AIR-LLM for two reasons. First, the channel effect applies to all the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} subcarriers of 𝐖\mathbf{W}, whereas the outputs 𝐘\mathbf{Y} are digitized only after the LPF has collapsed them into a single subcarrier, where the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} per-subcarrier channel matrices are already mixed together and no longer separable. Second, even if they were separable, applying (2) over the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} subcarriers would take 8​A2​Nfft8A^{2}N_{\textrm{fft}} FLOPs, approximately 2A×2A\times the cost of the 2​A2A IPs that it enables, overshadowing the energy savings that motivate AIR-LLM.

We design the CC calibration units on the edge device to calibrate the channel effect, as shown in Fig. 3.

3.3. Precoder and Postcoder Optimization

Putting (6), (7), (8), and (9) together, the ultimate goal of AIR-LLM is to minimize the mean squared error (MSE) between the final output signal 𝐲^′′\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime\prime} and the ground truth output signal 𝐲\mathbf{y} by optimizing the precoder PpreP_{\textrm{pre}} and postcoder PpostP_{\textrm{post}} jointly across all calibration units. We formulate this as the optimization problem in OPT-Orig.

blocks.html_en: Waiving the need of 𝐖\mathbf{W} and 𝐱\mathbf{x}.   Fortunately, we observe that 𝐲^a′′−𝐲a\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime\prime}_{a}-\mathbf{y}_{a} is bilinear in (𝐖,𝐱)(\mathbf{W},\mathbf{x}), so the expectation objective in OPT-Orig depends only on the first/second-order statistics of 𝐖\mathbf{W} and 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Hence, we assume that the entries of 𝐖\mathbf{W} and 𝐱\mathbf{x} are zero-mean and mutually independent, and i.i.d. within each; we also assume a high SNR region that ignores the noise term in (1). blocks.html_en: 3.4. System Efficiency Analysis
We analyze the efficiency of AIR-LLM along two dimensions: the airtime it occupies the wireless channel, and the energy it consumes on the edge device.

sentences.en: We analyze the efficiency of AIR-LLM along two dimensions: the airtime it occupies the wireless channel, and the energy it consumes on the edge device.

blocks.html_en: Airtime analysis.   The airtime of AIR-LLM is inversely proportional to the number of antennas AA and the occupied bandwidth BB. Interestingly, this form exactly follows a conventional communication link with spatial multiplexing on AA and frequency multiplexing on BB. On the other hand, AIR-LLM’s airtime is independent of the SNR, which instead determines the computing accuracy; AIR-LLM therefore does not customize the transmitted signals for each user, and is naturally fit to broadcasting. Leveraged by broadcasting, one transmission of the weights serves arbitrarily many edge users at a constant airtime, so the airtime amortized per user decreases as 1/U1/U. The complete analysis is given in Appendix C.3.

Leveraged by broadcasting, one transmission of the weights serves arbitrarily many edge users at a constant airtime, so the airtime amortized per user decreases as 1/U1/U.
The complete analysis is given in Appendix C.3.

blocks.html_en: Energy analysis.   Overall, AIR-LLM achieves good energy efficiency on RF computing, whose energy per FLOP is further averaged down as the GEMV scales up to LLM. This is because the energy consumption of almost every hardware component in AIR-LLM is amortized by either the input size NN or the output size MM, leaving the DAC, whose per-FLOP energy is set by the antenna number AA and the unit number CC, as the floor that a large GEMV converges to. Such a scaling law is contributed by two key designs. First, the RF mixer and the LPF collapse the whole input dimension into a single subcarrier with a downsampling ratio of NN, so the ADC takes only one sample per inner product, which usually dominates the energy budget of an analog computing system; the postcoding runs on that same single sample per antenna, so its energy is amortized by NN as well. Second, the precoding and the IFFT are paid only once per GEMV, as the same precoded input signal 𝐱′\mathbf{x}^{\prime} is reused across all the ⌈M/(2​A)⌉\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil rounds, so their energy is amortized by the output size MM. The per-component analysis is in Appendix C.4.

blocks.html_en: Tradeoff on computing accuracy, airtime, and energy.   The calibration unit number CC is where these three metrics meet. On the accuracy side, OPT-Chan calibrates the channel with a rank-CC approximation, so a larger CC leaves a smaller residual and thus a more accurate channel calibration; and the more antennas AA are deployed, the larger CC this accuracy requires. On the energy side, however, every energy term grows linearly with CC. Scaling up AA therefore shortens the airtime but pays for its accuracy in energy, so CC should be the smallest that meets the target task’s accuracy.

blocks.html_en: 4. Implementation
We implement AIR-LLM on the wireless channels of real-world urban scenes by a ray-tracing simulator, and on the distortion of a real RF mixer, measured on a wired testbed.
