blocks.html_en: 4.1. Channel Modeling by Ray Tracing

sentences.en: The two Sionna ray-tracing scenes in Paris (a) and Munich (b), and the testbed for RF mixer profiling.

blocks.html_en: Sionna ray-tracing simulator.   We build the wireless channel between the central radio and the edge devices on top of NVIDIA Sionna’s ray-tracing engine (v2.0.1) (Hoydis et al., 2022; Hoydis et al., 2023). Specifically, Sionna simulates the wireless signal propagation process by shooting 10710^{7} rays into a digital twin of a real-world city scene and resolving their interactions (e.g., reflection, refraction, and diffraction) with the buildings, grounds, etc. Assembling these propagation paths, it provides the realistic channel HH that the weight signal 𝐖\mathbf{W} propagates through to each of the edge devices. As shown in Fig. 4(a) and (b), we evaluate AIR-LLM in two contrasting urban scenes: (i) Place Charles de Gaulle in Paris, open enough that a line-of-sight (LOS) path always holds, and (ii) the city center of Munich, densely built so that multipath is rich while the LOS path is often blocked.

As shown in Fig. 4(a) and (b), we evaluate AIR-LLM in two contrasting urban scenes: (i) Place Charles de Gaulle in Paris, open enough that a line-of-sight (LOS) path always holds, and (ii) the city center of Munich, densely built so that multipath is rich while the LOS path is often blocked.

blocks.html_en: Central radio configuration.   The central radio sits at the center of each scene, 10 m above the ground. It carries AA antennas (A=4A=4 by default) on ⌈A/2⌉\left\lceil{A/2}\right\rceil physical elements, each of two orthogonal polarizations, spaced 1.7 m apart. It broadcasts the weight signal on the CBRS band (Sohul et al., 2015) at a 3.5 GHz carrier frequency over 100 MHz of bandwidth. The default broadcast power per antenna is set to 50 dBm, and the coverage radius is 100 m.

blocks.html_en: 4.2. Hardware Profiling on Real RF Mixer

sentences.en: Hardware Profiling on Real RF Mixer

blocks.html_en: RF mixers are not built for analog multiplication, and hence distort the desired product. We therefore measure the distortion of a real RF mixer, ZEM-4300+ (Mini-Circuits, 2024), driven by USRP X310 radios (Ettus Research, 2024) as the transceivers, as shown in Fig. 4(c). The profiling is wired, so the power entering the mixer stays far above the noise floor; the link is thus considered noiseless, and the computing errors are fully attributed to the mixer’s own distortion. Specifically, for each power at the mixer’s RF port, which receives the weight signal over the air in a deployment, we sweep the power at its LO port and keep the lowest distortion error, i.e., the best effective number of bits (ENOB), that the mixer reaches. The measured distortion ENOB curve over the RF power is shown in Fig. A2 of Appendix E.1. In our evaluation, we read this curve at each edge device’s received weight signal power and plug in the corresponding distortion error.

5.1. Benchmarking on GEMV

blocks.html_en: GEMV accuracy over the user PL.   Following the default setup in §4.1, Fig. 5 scatters the ENOB of a randomized GEMV by each of the 100 candidate users in Paris and Munich against their PLs. The ENOB generally decreases with the PL, as a higher PL lowers the power, and thus the SNR, of the weight signal arriving at the user. The open scene of Paris, where an LOS path is more likely and the PL is therefore lower (median 84.0 dB), reaches a median ENOB of 3.97 bit with 5/95-th percentiles of 1.58/5.69 bit, whereas the users of Munich, mostly without an LOS path (median 91.4 dB), reach only 2.91 bit with 0.53/5.33 bit. In addition, the PL does not determine the ENOB, which further depends on how the received power is spread over the multi-path components: within a PL of 89–91 dB alone, the ENOB still ranges over 2.01–5.33 bit. We empirically select the user with approximately 4.00 bit at 86.3 dB in Paris and that of approximately 3.00 bit at 94.1 dB in Munich, starred in the figure, as the default for the experiments below.

blocks.html_en: GEMV accuracy over the central radio power.   Fig. 5 sweeps the central radio transmit power from 30 dBm to 70 dBm on the two selected users. Both scenes follow the same two-stage trend: the ENOB first grows by roughly 1 bit per 10 dB of transmit power, and then saturates. Fig. 6 illustrates this trade-off in Paris on a single-round GEMV of M=2​AM=2A and N=4,096N={4,096}, sweeping C={1,2,…,A2}C=\left\{1,2,\dots,A^{2}\right\} at A={2,4,8,16,32}A=\left\{2,4,8,16,32\right\}, i.e., an airtime gain of 2/4/8/16/32×\times over WISE, with each array at the central radio power of 40/50/60/70/80 dBm.
Given AA, a larger CC compensates for the channel more accurately and is saturated at some point depending on the channel’s complexity.
At A=4A={4}, for example, the ENOB climbs from 0.55 bit at C=1C={1} to 3.97 at 8 units and 5.07 at 10; five further units then add only 0.43 bit while costing 1.5×\times the energy.

Fig. 6 extracts the minimum energy reaching each ENOB level, normalized to that by WISE: 3 bit costs 1.02/1.90/3.86/5.09/9.60×\times and 4 bit costs 1.54/2.44/5.86/6.96/13.59×\times at A=2/4/8/16/32A={2/4/8/16/32}.
This suggests that, to reduce the airtime with a larger AA, the same ENOB requires more energy consumption, because an A2A^{2}-entry per-subcarrier matrix takes more units to invert.
The same trends hold in Munich, whose results are shown in Appendix F.1.

blocks.html_en: Scaling up the GEMV size.   In Fig. 7, we scale up the GEMV’s input and output sizes together, over N=M={20,21,…,214}N=M=\left\{2^{0},2^{1},\dots,2^{14}\right\}. Up to N=M=23N=M=2^{3}, where a GEMV is completed within a single round, the computing accuracy stays at 5.58–5.75 bit in Paris and 3.85–3.94 bit in Munich. Beyond that point, where multiple rounds are needed, the ENOB drops slightly to 3.99–4.51 and 3.10–3.39 bit, respectively, which is maintained as the size keeps scaling up. AIR-LLM therefore supports good computing accuracy on the large-scale GEMVs that are widely used in LLMs. Fig. 7 further illustrates the energy per FLOP over the same sweep of GEMV scales, normalized to that of the FP16 baseline. That of FP16 and of the WoQ baselines, counting both the data movement and the digital computing, is constant over the sweep, with W4A16/W3A16 3.72/4.80×\times more energy efficient than FP16. In contrast, AIR-LLM’s energy per FLOP scales down as the GEMV scales up. A small GEMV is bottlenecked by the digital arithmetic of the precoding, the IFFT, and the postcoding (e.g., only 3.81×\times more energy efficient than FP16 at N=24N=2^{4}), after which the bottleneck moves to the DAC, whose per-FLOP cost is constant over the GEMV size (e.g., 50.2×\times more energy efficient than FP16 at N=212N=2^{12}). The ADC energy, which dominates conventional analog computing, is nearly free because of AIR-LLM’s downsampling ratio of NN. In applications whose GEMV input is itself an analog waveform, e.g., a received wireless signal or a biomedical sensor readout, this bottlenecked DAC energy is waived as well. This is exactly the regime an LLM runs in, whose inference is dominated by large GEMVs, and where AIR-LLM therefore costs the edge device the least.

blocks.html_en: 5.2. Benchmarking on LLM

We run whole LLMs with all weight-activation GEMVs computed in analog by AIR-LLM, and the remaining in digital. The LLM tasks and the WoQ/analog computing baselines are described in Appendix E.2 and E.3.

The LLM tasks and the WoQ/analog computing baselines are described in Appendix E.2 and E.3.

blocks.html_en: PPL on WikiText-2.   In Tab. 2, we present the WikiText-2 PPL at the sequence length of 2,048 over nine LLMs of four families: LLaMA-3.2 (1B and 3B), LLaMA-3.1 (8B and 70B), LLaMA-2 (7B and 13B), Mistral-7B, and Gemma-4 (E2B and E4B). The selected user in Paris, resolving about 4 bit, is read against the W4A16 baselines (RTN, GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023), and AWQ (Lin et al., 2024)) and the ENOB-4 analog computing baselines (AWGN and HyFlexPIM (Song et al., 2025)); the user in Munich, at about 3 bit, against their W3A16 and ENOB-3 counterparts. In Paris, specifically, AIR-LLM beats the best of the WoQ baselines on 7 out of the 9 LLMs, and the best of the analog computing baselines on 4 of the 9, staying within 5.6% of it on the other five. In Munich, where every baseline loses more at 3 bit, it beats the best of the W3A16 and of the ENOB-3 baselines on 7 and 5 of the 9, respectively. Such comparable or slightly lower PPLs show that the errors of AIR-LLM, including the thermal noise, the hardware distortion, and the imperfect channel compensation, still leave enough computing accuracy for an LLM inference.

blocks.html_en: Energy consumption per token.   Fig. 8 illustrates the per-token energy the edge device spends on the nine LLMs at the selected user in Paris, against four baselines that combine the remote/local weight storage with the FP16/W4A16 precision. All these energy consumptions are normalized to that of the remote FP16 on LLaMA-3.1-8B. On the same LLaMA-3.1-8B, AIR-LLM costs 157.7×\times and 40.4×\times less energy than the remote FP16 and W4A16, respectively, and against the local FP16 and W4A16, whose weights are more easily accessible from the device’s own memory, AIR-LLM still wins by 51.5×\times and 13.9×\times. Such an energy gain holds over all nine LLMs. Specifically for the two W4A16 baselines, whose PPL is comparable to AIR-LLM, AIR-LLM gains 35.4–44.0×\times against the remote one, owing to the downsampling ratio of NN at AIR-LLM’s ADC, as well as the much lighter digital pipeline behind it. AIR-LLM even achieves 12.9–14.3×\times against the local one, whose weights are easier to access than AIR-LLM’s, thanks to the waiving of the energy-expensive data movement. The Munich device draws the same conclusion against its own W3A16 baselines, as reported in Fig. A5.

blocks.html_en: Airtime per token.   In Paris, Fig. 9 presents the per-token airtime occupying the wireless channel, including AIR-LLM and the two remote baselines on the same nine LLMs. Similarly, the airtime is normalized to that of the remote FP16 on LLaMA-3.1-8B; the two local baselines occupy no channel and are therefore skipped. On LLaMA-3.1-8B, AIR-LLM takes 5.11×\times less airtime than the remote FP16 baseline, and slightly less airtime of 1.28×\times compared to the W4A16 baseline. Both ratios stay constant at 5.11×\times and 1.28×\times across all nine LLMs, as the airtime of AIR-LLM and that of the remote baselines are proportional to the same weight count. In this single-user case, the close airtime to the W4A16 baseline comes from the physical limit of the wireless channel (27): the airtime is scaled down linearly with the bandwidth BB and the antenna number AA for both the communication and AIR-LLM’s computing, and their remaining difference in the SNR is canceled out once the baseline is quantized to the specific weight width giving the close PPL performance to AIR-LLM. Similar ratios are also observed in Munich in Fig. A5 of Appendix F.2. In a dense-user scenario, however, AIR-LLM’s broadcasting capability significantly outperforms these WoQ baselines regarding the airtime, which is later shown in §5.4.

blocks.html_en: PPL over the sequence length.   In Tab. 3, we sweep the sequence length from 256 to 16,384 tokens to evaluate AIR-LLM’s robustness over the context length of the prefilling phase. The PPLs of the FP16 baseline and of AIR-LLM in Paris/Munich fall as the context grows, and AIR-LLM’s relative gap to the FP16 reference narrows and then flattens, spanning 3.9–6.6% and 17.1–25.3% over the sweep while settling at about 4.0% and 17.3% beyond 2,048 tokens. This suggests that AIR-LLM’s computing error does not accumulate along the context, and that the same robustness would potentially extend to the much longer contexts demanded by future LLM applications. Note that AIR-LLM’s per-token energy and airtime are constant along this axis, since both are dominated by streaming the weights of each layer once per token, independent of the token number.

blocks.html_en: 5.3. Impact of the System Factors
We examine more deployment factors, such as transmit power, antenna/calibration unit number, and frequency band.

sentences.en: We examine more deployment factors, such as transmit power, antenna/calibration unit number, and frequency band.
The PPL of AIR-LLM in Paris and Munich over different central radio broadcasting power.

blocks.html_en: Impact of the central radio transmit power.   We evaluate the impact of the transmit power under the same LLaMA-3.1-8B setup in Paris and Munich, which is presented in Tab. 4. The Paris user is already saturated at 35 dBm with 9.1% above the FP16 reference of 6.24, and raising the power to 60 dBm narrows that gap only to 3.8%. This hints that the computing error of this user comes from the imprecise channel calibration and the RF mixer’s imperfection. In comparison, the Munich user is still power-limited: its PPL stays orders of magnitude above the FP16 reference below 50 dBm, and then improves steeply to 8.8% at 60 dBm, meaning that its computing accuracy is mainly determined by the thermal noise. Both observations match the two-stage trend of Fig. 5. In AIR-LLM, users under different channel conditions are limited by different sources of the computing error, which in turn decides whether more transmit power pays off.

blocks.html_en: Performance in other bands.   We repeat the sweeps above in the 0.915 GHz ISM band with 25 MHz bandwidth, and the 28 GHz mmWave band with 400 MHz bandwidth, on the same two users in Paris/Munich, as summarized in Tab. 6. blocks.html_en: PPL over the edge users.   Fig. 10 marks the positions of the 20 edge users per scene, spanning PLs of 70.0–99.9 dB in Paris and 68.6–105.0 dB in Munich. We also label each user with its respective PPL on LLaMA-3.1-8B using AIR-LLM, and the CDFs are further given in Fig. 11. Specifically for Paris, the median PPL is 6.52, better than the W4A16 baseline of 6.65, and in Munich it is 7.23, better than the W3A16 baseline of 8.24; 70% and 80% of the users, respectively, fall below these two baselines. Note that one extreme user in Paris suffers an outlier PPL of 255.27. Despite its PL of 84.0 dB, its received power concentrates on too few multi-path components to support spatial multiplexing, which leaves its channel matrix HH nearly singular. Such a degradation also appears for the communication-based baselines whose channel capacity collapses on the same link; for AIR-LLM, it can be alleviated by falling back to fewer antennas AA, which trades the airtime for a better-conditioned HH.

blocks.html_en: Airtime over the edge users.   Fig. 12 plots the total airtime that one token takes while the first UU users are served. The communication baselines are based on unicasting, where every user is served separately at its own MCS customized to its channel quality. Thus, serving UU users costs U×U\times the airtime of a single user, and the total grows linearly. In comparison, AIR-LLM broadcasts the weights for the 20 users simultaneously, because the central radio is user-unaware and one uniform transmission is fed to every user inside the coverage. Therefore, the airtime of AIR-LLM is constant over UU, which is 104.1×\times/26.0×\times less than that by the FP16/W4A16 baselines with 20 users. Munich shows the same in Fig. A7 of Appendix F.4. This broadcast- and user-scalable feature lets AIR-LLM serve the thriving number of future edge users.

blocks.html_en: 6. Related Works

LLM accelerators.   Serving an LLM is memory-bounded by the weight movement rather than arithmetic (Guo et al., 2025). One category of works shrinks the bits per weight and co-designs the compute units around the resulting mixed-format GEMVs (Frantar et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2023; Tseng et al., 2024), with the hardware absorbing the outliers (Guo et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024) or the dequantization (Park et al., 2025; Mo et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026); a second attacks the movement rather than the format, placing the compute next to the memory that holds the weights and the KV cache (Park et al., 2024; Heo et al., 2024; Yun et al., 2024). All share one premise: the weights are already stored in the device’s memory, and only the cost of fetching and multiplying a resident weight is optimized. AIR-LLM removes that premise: no weight is stored on the edge device; each arrival of the broadcast weight waveform is consumed and computed directly in the RF/analog domain.

All share one premise: the weights are already stored in the device’s memory, and only the cost of fetching and multiplying a resident weight is optimized.
AIR-LLM removes that premise: no weight is stored on the edge device; each arrival of the broadcast weight waveform is consumed and computed directly in the RF/analog domain.

blocks.html_en: Analog computing for ML inference.   Analog computing performs the FLOPs in physics rather than in digital, escaping the energy floor of digital arithmetic: in-memory computing completes a GEMV on a ReRAM, PCM, or SRAM crossbar through Ohm’s and Kirchhoff’s laws (Shafiee et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2022; Le Gallo et al., 2023), while photonic computing multiplies operands encoded onto light (Shen et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2023). However, such designs are usually limited by their analog error and readout converters (Zhang et al., 2025; Khaddam-Aljameh et al., 2022), yet already carry real models at a handful of effective bits (Ambrogio et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024); AIR-LLM likewise reports every result at the effective bits its link resolves (Dettmers and Zettlemoyer, 2023). Closest in spirit is the work that lets operand delivery and computation happen in the same physical layer, over fiber (Sludds et al., 2022) or over the air (Reus-Muns et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2026b; Gao et al., 2026a), the latter inside a commodity receiver’s RF mixer; unlike over-the-air computation, which superposes many transmitters into a sum (Nazer and Gastpar, 2007; Zhu et al., 2020), AIR-LLM’s mixer forms a product of an arriving weight waveform with a local input. In addition, AIR-LLM generalizes the single-antenna and single-weight-stream into an A×AA\times A MIMO engine to largely reduce the airtime, whose calibration units zero-force a real, frequency-selective channel.

However, such designs are usually limited by their analog error and readout converters (Zhang et al., 2025; Khaddam-Aljameh et al., 2022), yet already carry real models at a handful of effective bits (Ambrogio et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024); AIR-LLM likewise reports every result at the effective bits its link resolves (Dettmers and Zettlemoyer, 2023).

In addition, AIR-LLM generalizes the single-antenna and single-weight-stream into an A×AA\times A MIMO engine to largely reduce the airtime, whose calibration units zero-force a real, frequency-selective channel.

blocks.html_en: LLM deployment on the edge.   On-device LLM serving is a capacity problem before a compute one, and the systems response keeps as few weights resident as possible: pruning (Niu et al., 2020), activation sparsity (Song et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024), flash streaming (Alizadeh et al., 2024), or accelerator–model co-design (Yu et al., 2024). Yet even a quantized resident model stays memory-bound on commodity phones, where energy and thermals make continuous generation untenable (Laskaridis et al., 2024). The complementary response moves the model off the device (Kwon et al., 2023; Stojkovic et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2017), trading the memory wall for a per-query network cost and for handing the prompt to the server. Both leave each device paying, privately and per token, for the same weights that every other device in the cell also pays for (Qu et al., 2024). AIR-LLM instead disaggregates the weight storage to the central radio while keeping both the computation and the prompt on the edge, and because its transmission is edge-device-unaware, one broadcast is mixed by every device in the coverage at once, amortizing the delivery cost over the devices served. Such one-to-many analog delivery has precedent in SoftCast (Jakubczak and Katabi, 2011), which broadcasts video over raw OFDM at a fidelity set by each receiver’s own channel.

blocks.html_en: 7. Conclusion

In this paper, we present AIR-LLM, an LLM inference architecture for edge users that is memory-access-free, user-scalable and energy-efficient. Specifically, AIR-LLM exploits MIMO spatial multiplexing to deliver multiple weight streams at a time and thereby shorten the airtime, and the design of the precoder–postcoder pair on the edge user energy-efficiently calibrates its own wireless channel. Exhaustive evaluations on the NVIDIA Sionna ray-traced channels and the profiling of a real RF mixer reveal that, with a slight PPL gap to the FP16 baseline, AIR-LLM cuts the per-token energy and airtime by orders of magnitude. We believe AIR-LLM opens up a new path for the next generation of edge intelligence.

blocks.html_en: Appendix B Blocked Correlation Operation
We generalize the linear-convolution mapping into a blocked correlation operation (BCO), where the mixer retains a whole output block of subcarriers rather than a single one.

blocks.html_en: Implication on the calibration units.   The calibration unit of §3.3 carries over unchanged, with one structural caveat on the precoder. Under BCO, the LL subcarriers within a block jointly carry one correlation, so they must be scaled identically: a per-subcarrier precoder would reweight the individual correlation taps and destroy the block structure of (14). The precoder is therefore constant within each block, i.e., Ppre∈ℂC×DP_{\textrm{pre}}\in\mathbb{C}^{C\times D} with the subcarrier kk driven by Ppre​[c,⌊k/L⌋]P_{\textrm{pre}}[c,\left\lfloor{k/L}\right\rfloor], which is precisely the form optimized in (17) of §B.2. The postcoder, in contrast, acts across antennas only and is applied identically to all subcarriers, so it is unaffected. For a GEMV, L=1L=1 makes the per-block and the per-subcarrier precoder identical, recovering the main-body design.

blocks.html_en: B.3. Convergence of the Optimization

We study how the two-step solve converges on the GEMV, i.e., the degenerate case L=1L=1 in which (17) reduces to the OPT-Chan of §3.3. The two edge devices are the selected users of Paris and Munich of §5.1, resolving approximately 4.00 and 3.00 bit, so the numbers below are directly comparable to the evaluation.

sentences.en: We study how the two-step solve converges on the GEMV, i.e., the degenerate case L=1L=1 in which (17) reduces to the OPT-Chan of §3.3.
The two edge devices are the selected users of Paris and Munich of §5.1, resolving approximately 4.00 and 3.00 bit, so the numbers below are directly comparable to the evaluation.

blocks.html_en: What each step buys.   Fig. A1 traces the two steps on the selected edge device of each scene. Before either of them, the raw link is unusable: fitting the single complex gain that an AGC and a carrier recovery already provide leaves 0.00 bit in Paris and 0.05 bit in Munich, i.e., the frequency selectivity of HH and its inter-antenna mixing alone destroy the GEMV. The closed-form Step-1 initialization recovers most of it at once, cutting the loss of (17) from 0.998 to 0.013 in Paris and from 0.947 to 0.259 in Munich, i.e., to 3.12 and 0.97 bit. The gap between the two scenes is the price of the per-block channel approximation of (19): the richer multipath of Munich makes the frequency response vary within a block, so the averaged H¯\bar{H} that Step 1 inverts sits further from the per-subcarrier channel that (17) actually scores, and the SVD initialization alone is worth about one bit there against three in Paris.

blocks.html_en: How many ALS iterations.   Figs. A1 and A1 answer how long Step 2 has to run. A single ALS pass recovers most of what Step 1 leaves behind, dropping the loss by a further 2.7×\times in Paris and 17.5×\times in Munich to reach 3.79 and 2.85 bit. Everything after that pass is a slow creep: iterations 2 through 10 add only 0.13 bit in Paris and 0.29 bit in Munich, and the relative-tolerance test stops the two devices at 40 and 22 iterations, at 4.08 and 3.13 bit. Since one iteration is two closed-form least-squares solves and the optimization runs once per channel coherence time rather than per GEMV, we run it to that convergence throughout the evaluation, though stopping after the first pass would already sit within 0.29 bit of it.

blocks.html_en: Appendix C Airtime and Energy Consumption

sentences.en: Appendix C Airtime and Energy Consumption

blocks.html_en: This section analyzes the two efficiency metrics of AIR-LLM, the airtime and the energy consumption per FLOP. We derive them at the general block size of a BCO (§C.1 and §C.2), and then substitute the GEMV mapping of the main body, its degenerate case, to read off the airtime and the energy of a GEMV (§C.3 and §C.4).

sentences.en: This section analyzes the two efficiency metrics of AIR-LLM, the airtime and the energy consumption per FLOP.

We derive them at the general block size of a BCO (§C.1 and §C.2), and then substitute the GEMV mapping of the main body, its degenerate case, to read off the airtime and the energy of a GEMV (§C.3 and §C.4).

blocks.html_en: C.1. Airtime of a BCO

We analyze the airtime of AIR-LLM, i.e., how long the RF chain of an edge device is occupied to compute one FLOP. It is bottlenecked by the duration of the signals, both the wireless one carrying 𝐖\mathbf{W} from the central radio and the local one carrying 𝐱\mathbf{x}, which the bandwidth BB sets.

blocks.html_en: C.2. Energy Consumption of a BCO

We analyze the edge-device-side energy consumption of AIR-LLM per FLOP by its complexity, i.e., the number of operations on three kinds of hardware, each costing a constant energy per operation: the DAC and the ADC, counted in samples, and the digital computing, counted in FLOPs.

blocks.html_en: Appendix D AIR-LLM in CNN

Convolutional (CONV) layers, which dominate CNNs, do not fit the one-subcarrier-per-output mapping of the main body: reusing the same kernel across all I2I^{2} positions of an image would require re-transmitting that kernel once per output pixel, so the broadcast weight traffic, the very resource AIR-LLM is built to save, would grow by I2I^{2}. The BCO of Appendix B removes that restriction, as one mixing round now retains a whole output block instead of a single subcarrier, and a kernel broadcast once is correlated against every position of the image within it. We map a Conv2D layer onto the BCO (§D.1), and then specialize the BCO airtime of §C.1 and the BCO energy of §C.2 to it (§D.2 and §D.3).

sentences.en: Convolutional (CONV) layers, which dominate CNNs, do not fit the one-subcarrier-per-output mapping of the main body: reusing the same kernel across all I2I^{2} positions of an image would require re-transmitting that kernel once per output pixel, so the broadcast weight traffic, the very resource AIR-LLM is built to save, would grow by I2I^{2}.

The BCO of Appendix B removes that restriction, as one mixing round now retains a whole output block instead of a single subcarrier, and a kernel broadcast once is correlated against every position of the image within it.
We map a Conv2D layer onto the BCO (§D.1), and then specialize the BCO airtime of §C.1 and the BCO energy of §C.2 to it (§D.2 and §D.3).

blocks.html_en: D.1. Mapping Conv2D onto BCO

Layer formulation.   We examine a general Conv2D layer with a kernel size of K×KK\times K, an image size of I×II\times I, NN input channels, and MM output channels, so that 𝐖(CONV)∈ℝN×M×K×K\mathbf{W}^{\textrm{(CONV)}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M\times K\times K}, 𝐗(CONV)∈ℝN×I×I\mathbf{X}^{\textrm{(CONV)}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times I\times I}, and 𝐘(CONV)∈ℝM×I×I\mathbf{Y}^{\textrm{(CONV)}}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times I\times I}. We assume KK is odd and that the correlation is zero-padded to preserve the image size. Just as a GEMV decomposes into MM inner products, this Conv2D decomposes into MM independent sub-convolutions, one per output channel, each of which becomes one BCO; as the layer is real-valued whereas the BCO is complex-valued, two output channels are packed into the real and the imaginary parts of a single BCO, as the two IPs of (4) are.

blocks.html_en: Takeaways.   Two opposite trends are visible in Tab. A5. On the one hand, the ADC and the cross-unit-summation terms both carry 1/N1/N and vanish as the layer deepens, exactly as in the GEMV case of Tab. A4: one ADC sample and one cross-unit addition now serve an entire input channel of the image rather than a single weight element, which is the saving that the reduced output bandwidth B/DB/D buys and that the remote baseline cannot obtain. The DAC term likewise decays as 1/K21/K^{2}, mirroring the airtime gain of (33). On the other hand, the digital encoding and decoding terms do not cancel as cleanly. Each of them does carry an amortization of its own, the transmitter-side precoding and IFFT over MM and the receiver-side FFT and postcoding over NN, so all three dimensions of §C.4 survive the Conv2D mapping intact. What survives with them, however, is a logarithmic factor the GEMV mapping does not have: the IFFT over all N​I2NI^{2} subcarriers and the receive FFT over the I2I^{2} subcarriers of a block leave a residual log2⁡(N​I)\log_{2}(NI) and log2⁡I\log_{2}I that both grow with the image size. Consequently, unlike the airtime of §D.2, where a larger kernel or image is strictly beneficial, the energy of Conv2D trades the analog savings on the converters against the digital cost of the wider OFDM symbol, and the two must be weighed together when choosing AIR-LLM’s operating point.

This section details the baselines, the tasks, and the metrics of the evaluation, together with the two measurements that the implementation of §4 rests on: the distortion profile of the RF mixer (Fig. A2) and the path-loss distribution of each ray-traced scene (Fig. A3).

blocks.html_en: E.1. Measured Distortion and Path Loss

Distortion profile of the RF mixer.   Fig. A2 reports the wired sweep of §4: at each power delivered to the mixer’s RF port, the LO power is swept and the best ENOB is kept. The ENOB climbs with the RF power and then flattens as the mixer’s own nonlinearity takes over from the drive level; this knee is the distortion floor that the saturated users of §5.3 sit on.

blocks.html_en: Path loss across the candidate devices.   Fig. A3 shows the PL distribution of the 100 candidate devices dropped in each scene, from which the representative devices of §5.1 are selected. The open scene of Paris is tightly concentrated, a single mode of median 84.0 dB with 5/95-th percentiles of 74.9/97.8 dB, since almost every drop keeps an LOS path to the central radio. The dense scene of Munich is both worse and far wider, a median of 91.4 dB and percentiles of 75.2/131.3 dB, with a long shadowed tail of devices whose LOS path is blocked by a building. Both scenes therefore span the range of link qualities from the noise-limited users of §5.3 to the distortion-limited ones.

blocks.html_en: E.2. Baselines
We benchmark AIR-LLM against digital baselines along two dimensions: the precision at which the weights are kept, and the weight storage from which they reach the edge device.

sentences.en: We benchmark AIR-LLM against digital baselines along two dimensions: the precision at which the weights are kept, and the weight storage from which they reach the edge device.

blocks.html_en: Precision dimension.   We take FP16 as the exact reference, and further consider weight-only quantization (WoQ) at 4/3 bit, i.e., W4A16 and W3A16, by RTN, GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023), and AWQ (Lin et al., 2024).

sentences.en: We take FP16 as the exact reference, and further consider weight-only quantization (WoQ) at 4/3 bit, i.e., W4A16 and W3A16, by RTN, GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023), and AWQ (Lin et al., 2024).

blocks.html_en: Analog computing baselines.   We further benchmark against two analog computing baselines at the same ENOB as AIR-LLM’s device: (i) AWGN, additive Gaussian noise on each GEMV output, and (ii) HyFlexPIM, a multiplicative Gaussian error on each weight, i.e., the conductance spread of a memristive crossbar. The former error is redrawn per GEMV, whereas the latter is frozen on the weights; AIR-LLM sits in between, as its thermal noise is redrawn per transmission while its calibration residual and mixer distortion hold for as long as the channel does.

The former error is redrawn per GEMV, whereas the latter is frozen on the weights; AIR-LLM sits in between, as its thermal noise is redrawn per transmission while its calibration residual and mixer distortion hold for as long as the channel does.

blocks.html_en: Weight storage dimension.   Under remote storage, the weights are kept on the central radio and delivered to the edge device over the same wireless channel as AIR-LLM’s by a standard communication link. Under local storage, they are instead pre-stored in the edge device’s memory. AIR-LLM targets the remote storage, which is both more realistic for edge computing and more challenging than the local one.

blocks.html_en: Airtime and energy consumption.   We further report the airtime and the energy consumption per token. The airtime is the time one token occupies the wireless link, the resource the central radio rations across the edge devices it serves; for the remote storage baselines, it is counted on the same ray-traced channel under a standard-compliant 5G NR link (3GPP, 2022a; 3GPP, 2022b), while the local storage baselines occupy no airtime. The energy consumption is based on the per-operation energies of state-of-the-art DACs (Olieman et al., 2015), ADCs (Harpe et al., 2011; Murmann, 2026), digital computing (NVIDIA, 2024), and data movement (Antepara et al., 2025).

blocks.html_en: Energy and airtime per token in Munich.   Fig. A5 repeats Figs. 8 and 9 on the selected device of Munich, whose roughly 3 bit of end-to-end resolution reads it against the W3A16 baselines. The energy conclusion of §5.2 carries over unchanged: on LLaMA-3.1-8B, AIR-LLM costs 165.5×\times and 32.1×\times less energy than the remote FP16 and W3A16 baselines, and 51.5×\times and 10.7×\times less than the two local ones, holding at 28.3–35.3×\times and 10.0–11.1×\times against the two W3A16 baselines over all nine LLMs. That the gain against the local FP16 baseline is exactly the 51.5×\times of Paris is no coincidence: AIR-LLM’s per-token energy is set by its own DAC, digital pipeline, and unit number, none of which depends on the channel, and a local baseline pays data movement rather than airtime, so neither side of that ratio moves with the scene. The airtime does move, and it moves in AIR-LLM’s favor: the remote FP16 baseline takes 5.37–5.42×\times AIR-LLM’s airtime here against 5.11×\times in Paris, since the worse link costs the communication baseline capacity while AIR-LLM’s signal duration is fixed by BB and AA alone (27). The quantized baseline, in contrast, closes to 1.01–1.02×\times from the 1.28×\times that W4A16 leaves in Paris: a quarter fewer bits per weight is enough to offset the capacity its own link costs it.

blocks.html_en: What each edge device generates.   Fig. A6 and Tabs. A6 and A7 put the PPLs of §5.4 next to what the model actually writes: each of the 20 devices per scene continues one shared prompt, with every GEMV of LLaMA-3.1-8B carried over that device’s own ray-traced channel. The rows fall by ENOB, and the degradation along them is graded rather than abrupt. Above about 3.5 bit, which 16 of the 20 devices reach in Paris and 8 in Munich, the continuations are fluent and name the city’s real landmarks, differing from the FP16 reference in which true fact they pick rather than in whether they pick one at all. Below it they stay grammatical but drift into invented detail and begin to repeat themselves, e.g., device 3 of Paris at 3.21 bit dates a fountain to 1772 and device 11 of Munich at 3.16 bit loops on its beer gardens, while their PPLs are still only 7.99 and 7.27. Only under about 2.5 bit do they collapse: device 18 of Paris restarts the prompt verbatim at 2.52 bit, device 4 of Munich does the same at 2.49 bit, and device 11 of Paris, the near-singular channel of §5.4, degenerates into repeated tokens at 2.00 bit and the outlying PPL of 255.27. This is the practical reading of the CDFs in Fig. 11: AIR-LLM degrades an LLM gracefully over most of a coverage zone, and the devices it fails are the few whose channel is too poorly conditioned to invert rather than the ones that are merely far away: device 12 of Munich, the most distant of all 40 at 105.0 dB, still resolves 4.19 bit and reads a PPL of 6.60.

Below it they stay grammatical but drift into invented detail and begin to repeat themselves, e.g., device 3 of Paris at 3.21 bit dates a fountain to 1772 and device 11 of Munich at 3.16 bit loops on its beer gardens, while their PPLs are still only 7.99 and 7.27.

Only under about 2.5 bit do they collapse: device 18 of Paris restarts the prompt verbatim at 2.52 bit, device 4 of Munich does the same at 2.49 bit, and device 11 of Paris, the near-singular channel of §5.4, degenerates into repeated tokens at 2.00 bit and the outlying PPL of 255.27.

This is the practical reading of the CDFs in Fig. 11: AIR-LLM degrades an LLM gracefully over most of a coverage zone, and the devices it fails are the few whose channel is too poorly conditioned to invert rather than the ones that are merely far away: device 12 of Munich, the most distant of all 40 at 105.0 dB, still resolves 4.19 bit and reads a PPL of 6.60.

blocks.html_en: Zero-shot accuracy using LLaMA-3.1-8B.   We evaluate AIR-LLM and the same set of baselines on LLaMA-3.1-8B’s inference on six commonsense-reasoning benchmarks, as shown in Tab. A8. This metric is harsher on analog computing than the PPL, because of how it is scored: every candidate continuation is concatenated to the same stem and run through its own inference pass, and the answer is the candidate with the highest log-likelihood. An error that is deterministic given the weights, the quantization grid of WoQ or the frozen conductance spread of HyFlexPIM, shifts all the candidates of a question in the same direction, so the comparison among them, and thus the argmax, largely survives. A non-deterministic one does not: the AWGN baseline and AIR-LLM’s thermal noise are redrawn independently in every pass, so each candidate is scored under its own realization of the error, and the choice flips whenever that perturbation exceeds the log-likelihood margin between the candidates. AWGN pays for this in full, collapsing to the chance level on all six tasks (37.98% at ENOB 4 and 36.30% at ENOB 3) despite an ENOB matched to AIR-LLM’s, whereas the weight-frozen HyFlexPIM stays within 0.42 points of the FP16 reference at ENOB 4. AIR-LLM sits between the two, averaging 68.72% in Paris and 65.67% in Munich against the 75.00% FP16 reference, as only its thermal noise is redrawn per transmission while its channel-calibration residual and the mixer’s distortion hold across the candidates of a question: Paris sits inside the W3A16 band (66.00–69.96%) and Munich 0.33 points below its weakest member. Task by task, the degradation is mild where the margins between the candidate continuations are wide (77.85%/75.39% on HellaSwag against 78.89%, and 81.13%/75.20% on BoolQ against 81.96%), and the average is dominated by WinoGrande (57.77%/57.14% against 73.56%), whose two candidates differ in a single pronoun referent and whose log-likelihood margin is therefore the narrowest of the six, so a few bits of analog error are enough to flip the choice.

blocks.html_en: F.3. Impact of the System Factors

Impact of repeating the weight signal.   The central radio may send the same weight signal several times and let the edge device average the copies, which trades airtime for a lower thermal noise: repeating it nn times costs nn times the airtime and lowers the noise power by 10​log10​n10\log_{10}n dB, while leaving the receive chain’s own distortion untouched. Tab. A9 sweeps this knob under the same LLaMA-3.1-8B setup as Tab. 4, where the last column measures the distortion floor that no repetition count can pass. The Paris user does not move at all, staying at 6.49 from a single copy to the floor, which confirms the same conclusion as its flat row in Tab. 4: this user is already limited by the channel calibration and the RF mixer rather than by the noise. The noise-limited Munich user does improve, but slowly: 16 copies, i.e., 16 times the airtime, buy 7.37 to 7.19, only 2.4% and already within 0.3% of its 7.17 floor. Repetition is therefore a much worse deal than the transmit power for the same user, which buys 7.9% over the same 10 dB in Tab. 4 at no airtime cost, and we keep a single copy of the weight signal throughout the other evaluations.

blocks.html_en: Impact of the carrier frequency.   We repeat the transmit power sweep of Tab. 4 in two other bands, the 915 MHz ISM band over 25 MHz and the 28 GHz mmWave band over 400 MHz, on the same two edge devices at the same positions and under the same LLaMA-3.1-8B setup, as shown in Tab. A10. The channels are re-traced at each carrier with the same scenes, whose ITU-R P.2040 material models are extrapolated below their 1 GHz lower edge for 915 MHz, and the noise floor follows the bandwidth of each band. Since the path loss of the two devices drops by 12 dB at 915 MHz and grows by 32 dB (Paris) and 41 dB (Munich) at 28 GHz, the power axis is shifted accordingly, with the regulatory ceilings of 36 dBm EIRP in the ISM band and 75 dBm per 100 MHz at 28 GHz inside the swept range. In the ISM band, both devices reach the accuracy of the paper’s operating point at 20 dB less power: Munich reads 7.28 at 30 dBm against the 7.37 that Tab. 4 measures at 50 dBm, while Paris has already saturated at 6.72. Both therefore stay usable inside the regulatory ceiling, reading 6.70 and 6.74 at 35 dBm, and the band’s own floors (6.69 in Paris and 6.44 in Munich) even reverse the two devices’ order, the lower carrier reaching the more distant device better than the nearer one. What the band costs is airtime: its 25 MHz is a quarter of the bandwidth BB that (26) divides, so every GEMV occupies four times the air.

content_html_zh:

抽象的。

Next-generation large language models (LLMs) are expanding from the cloud to ubiquitous edge devices. However, edge devices typically either lack the memory to store increasingly large LLM weights or, even with enough memory, spend unaffordable energy on loading the weights. This raises our question: can an edge device run an LLM without storing or loading its weights, but receive them over the air and consume them on the fly? Inspired by wireless broadcasting, we present AIR-LLM, an LLM inference architecture for edge devices, which is composed of: (i) a central radio (e.g., 5G base stations) that broadcasts the LLM weights into the air, and (ii) the edge user that receives the weights and completes the general matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) of LLM inference directly in the radio frequency (RF) domain using RF mixers. To further shorten the airtime, AIR-LLM exploits MIMO spatial multiplexing and proposes an energy-efficient precoder–postcoder pair on the edge to calibrate its own wireless channel. Since the central radio stays user-unaware, AIR-LLM is user-scalable so that one broadcast serves unlimited users within its coverage. We implement AIR-LLM on the NVIDIA Sionna ray-traced channels of two real-world urban scenes and the profiling of a real RF mixer. With a WikiText-2 perplexity degradation of 4.0% on LLaMA-3.1-8B, AIR-LLM saves the energy by 157.7×\times/40.4×\times against the FP16 and weight-only quantization baselines; with 20 users, its airtime is 104.1×\times/26.0×\times shorter, respectively.

Keywords:

LLM inference, edge computing, RF computing, RF mixer, weight broadcasting, MIMO communication

1. 介绍

Trillions of edge devices today are embracing emerging machine learning (ML) techniques for a wide range of applications, such as continuous health monitoring (Abbaspourazad et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2025), on-device speech recognition (Radford et al., 2023; Yazdani et al., 2016), and cooperative autonomous driving (Hu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2021). Among these, the emerging large language models (LLMs) provide a unique capability, allowing understanding, reasoning, and generating natural language (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Touvron et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023; Gemma Team, 2026). However, the usage of LLMs on the edge mostly relies on cloud computing, where the locally generated prompts are uploaded to a cloud server, and the responses are downloaded afterwards. This again exposes two typical concerns of cloud computing: the privacy of the sensitive prompts, as well as the round-trip latency, especially when the number of edge users is scaled up (Kang et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2025).

The key challenge that hinders such an on-device deployment lies in the daunting model size of today’s LLMs. For example, LLaMA-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) occupies 16 GB in FP16, and still 4 GB after 4-bit weight-only quantization (WoQ) (Frantar et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024). Such a model size stresses an edge device in two stages. First, its memory is typically too small to hold the whole model, so a local deployment has to keep downloading the weights and discarding them afterwards. Second, even if an edge device could store such an LLM entirely, the energy of loading the weights from memory to the computing unit is unaffordable. This is because LLM inference is memory-bounded, especially during the decoding phase, where fetching one weight feeds only two floating-point operations (FLOPs) (Guo et al., 2025). The weight movement therefore dominates the energy, much more than the arithmetic it feeds (Antepara et al., 2025; NVIDIA, 2024).

To overcome this, various computing paradigms have been proposed recently. For example, in-memory computing completes the computing in analog within the memory itself, on a ReRAM (Shafiee et al., 2016; Chi et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2022), PCM (Khaddam-Aljameh et al., 2022; Le Gallo et al., 2023), or SRAM (Liu et al., 2026) crossbar, so that the weights are never fetched. Over-the-air computing (Nazer and Gastpar, 2007; Zhu et al., 2020), in turn, superposes the signals of many transmitters over the wireless channel, so that the summation is completed by the channel itself. However, in both cases the size of the general matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) is frozen and limited by the hardware complexity, e.g., a crossbar of 128×\times128 cells (Shafiee et al., 2016) and an array of a few dozen antennas (Reus-Muns et al., 2023). Such a limited GEMV size is naturally incompatible with the LLM whose GEMV sizes keep increasing.

Our motivation lies in the wireless network these edge users already live in. Taking 5G networks as an example, a 5G base station already establishes wireless links to each edge user under its coverage. For these users, accessing the LLM weights is read-only, and thus a purely downlink process; once they run the same LLM, it is exactly what broadcasting was invented for: one transmission simultaneously serving every user in the coverage. Moreover, we employ radio-frequency (RF) computing (Gao et al., 2026b; Gao et al., 2026a), which completes the computing in RF via the passive RF mixer that every receiver already carries. The computing is thereby finished in analog once the broadcast signal arrives, without the weights ever being digitized into the local memory.

As shown in Fig. 1, we present AIR-LLM, an LLM inference architecture with (i) a central radio (e.g., a 5G base station) that frequency-encodes the LLM weights onto the subcarriers of an orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) waveform and broadcasts it, and (ii) any edge device in the coverage receives that waveform and computes on it inside its own RF front-end. The key computing component is the RF mixer every wireless device already carries: it multiplies its two inputs in the time domain, corresponding to a linear convolution in the frequency domain. Specifically, driving its local oscillator (LO) with a waveform encoding the activations therefore convolves the arriving weight spectrum with the activation spectrum, and the very middle subcarrier of this convolution is exactly the inner product of the weight and activation vectors. A comparison of existing computing paradigms is presented in Tab. 1.

On top of this principle, AIR-LLM makes two designs. First, it exploits A×AA\times A multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) spatial multiplexing, which delivers AA weight streams at a time and thus shortens the airtime by A×A\times. Second, it calibrates the MIMO channel with CC calibration units, each pairing a per-subcarrier precoder and a per-antenna postcoder, which compensates for the channel at a cost far below an explicit inversion, keeping the energy low.

Delivering the weights this way also fits broadcasting better than conventional communication in two aspects. First, AIR-LLM needs no handshake with users, as the computation is inherently tolerant to the errors introduced by thermal noise. In addition, its weight waveform stays identical regardless of the users’ SNRs, so no per-user modulation and coding scheme (MCS) is needed either.

We implement AIR-LLM on ray-traced channels of two urban scenes, Paris and Munich, and profile a real RF mixer, running nine LLMs from 1B to 70B parameters end-to-end with every weight-activation GEMV in RF computing. On LLaMA-3.1-8B and a selected user in the scene of Paris, AIR-LLM degrades the WikiText-2 perplexity (PPL) by only 4.0%, while cutting the per-token energy by 157.7×\times/40.4×\times against FP16/4-bit weight baselines with remote weight storage, and by 51.5×\times/13.9×\times against fetching them from local memory; with 20 users, its per-token airtime is 104.1×\times/26.0×\times shorter than FP16 and 4-bit WoQ.

We summarize the contribution of AIR-LLM as below.

  • • We propose AIR-LLM, a new computing paradigm for LLM inference on the edge, which is memory-access-free, user-scalable, and energy-efficient.
  • • We design an RF computing engine that shortens the airtime with MIMO spatial multiplexing, while maintaining the computing accuracy and energy efficiency.
  • • We evaluate AIR-LLM on Sionna ray-tracing and real RF mixer profiling, showing its near-lossless PPL on LLM tasks with orders-of-magnitude less energy and airtime.

2. 预赛

2.1. OFDM and MIMO Channel Model

OFDM signal structure. The signals are based on orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM), characterized by the FFT size NfftN_{\textrm{fft}}, i.e., the number of subcarriers in the frequency domain, and the occupied bandwidth BB. The resulting subcarrier spacing is Δ​f=B/Nfft\Delta f=B/N_{\textrm{fft}}.

MIMO signal notation. We consider an At×ArA^{t}\times A^{r} MIMO system, where AtA^{t} denotes the number of transmitting antennas on the central radio and ArA^{r} denotes the number of receiving antennas on each edge device. On the central radio side, the transmitted signals in the frequency domain are denoted by a complex-valued matrix St∈ℂAt×NfftS^{t}\in\mathbb{C}^{A^{t}\times N_{\textrm{fft}}}, whose ata^{t}-th row St[at,:]S^{t}[a^{t},:] gives the signal transmitted by the ata^{t}-th antenna. The received signals in the frequency domain are similarly denoted by Sr∈ℂAr×NfftS^{r}\in\mathbb{C}^{A^{r}\times N_{\textrm{fft}}}, whose ara^{r}-th row Sr[ar,:]S^{r}[a^{r},:] gives the signal received by the ara^{r}-th antenna.

2.2. Analog GEMV via RF Mixers

An RF mixer is a fundamental component on edge devices for up/down conversion. Essentially, it performs analog multiplication in the time domain, corresponding to the linear convolution in the frequency domain, where OFDM signals reside. Such a convolution operation can be leveraged for GEMV in ML inference.

Complex-valued linear convolution. The complex-valued nature of wireless signals allows an RF mixer to perform, in analog, the complex-valued linear convolution (denoted by ∗\ast) between two input signals of equal subcarrier spacing Δ​f\Delta f. This process yields the output activation signal Y∈ℂ2​Nfft−1Y\in\mathbb{C}^{2N_{\textrm{fft}}-1} as

3. RF Computing Engine

In this section, we present the RF computing engine of AIR-LLM on the edge device based on MIMO, as shown in Fig. 2, where AIR-LLM calibrates the channel of the broadcast weights with a pair of precoder and postcoder that are compatible with the RF mixer-driven analog GEMV.

3.1. Problem Formulation

We first introduce the basic configuration of the MIMO channel modeling, and then formulate the problem of designing the edge device hardware.

GEMV decoupling and IP parallelization. In AIR-LLM, we consider an A×AA\times A MIMO system for any central radio and edge device pair. This supports up to AA parallel spatial streams, each carrying an IP pair of (4), so that one round of AIR-LLM completes 2​A2A IPs and a GEMV takes ⌈M/(2​A)⌉\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil rounds. For these 2​A2A IPs per round, we denote the weight signals by 𝐖={𝐰a}\mathbf{W}=\{\mathbf{w}_{a}\} and the shared input signal by 𝐱\mathbf{x}, all spanning the Nfft=NN_{\textrm{fft}}=N subcarriers, i.e., 𝐰a,𝐱∈ℂNfft\mathbf{w}_{a},\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\textrm{fft}}}; their outputs are denoted by 𝐘={𝐲a}\mathbf{Y}=\{\mathbf{y}_{a}\} with 𝐲a∈ℂ\mathbf{y}_{a}\in\mathbb{C}.

MIMO channel modeling. In AIR-LLM, we let the central radio broadcast signals 𝐖\mathbf{W} with 𝐰a\mathbf{w}_{a} by the aa-th antenna without precoding. For a specific edge device with a channel H∈ℂA×A×NfftH\in\mathbb{C}^{A\times A\times N_{\textrm{fft}}}, the received signals are denoted by 𝐖′={𝐰a′}\mathbf{W}^{\prime}=\{\mathbf{w}^{\prime}_{a}\} with 𝐰a′∈ℂNfft\mathbf{w}^{\prime}_{a}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\textrm{fft}}} received by the aa-th antenna. This signal transmission process directly follows the MIMO channel model in (1), with At=Ar=AA^{t}=A^{r}=A.

Channel calibration challenges. The design of the central radio is edge device-unaware, i.e., does not incorporate any information specific to a particular edge device (e.g., its channel), so that its broadcasting can be generalized for any edge device within its coverage. In this case, the channel effect on 𝐖\mathbf{W} should be entirely calibrated at the edge device side. However, the conventional channel calibration in (2) is not feasible for AIR-LLM for two reasons. First, the channel effect applies to all the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} subcarriers of 𝐖\mathbf{W}, whereas the outputs 𝐘\mathbf{Y} are digitized only after the LPF has collapsed them into a single subcarrier, where the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} per-subcarrier channel matrices are already mixed together and no longer separable. Second, even if they were separable, applying (2) over the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} subcarriers would take 8​A2​Nfft8A^{2}N_{\textrm{fft}} FLOPs, approximately 2A×2A\times the cost of the 2​A2A IPs that it enables, overshadowing the energy savings that motivate AIR-LLM.

3.2. Edge Calibration Unit Design

We design the CC calibration units on the edge device to calibrate the channel effect, as shown in Fig. 3.

Calibration unit architecture. Generally, a calibration unit takes the digital signal 𝐱\mathbf{x} as input, which is (i) precoded and IFFTed in digital, (ii) split and duplicated into AA ways in analog, (iii) respectively mixed with the analog received signals 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime} across the AA antennas and low-pass filtered, and (iv) postcoded in digital. The key design of this calibration unit is the precoding on the 𝐱\mathbf{x} and the postcoding on the 𝐘\mathbf{Y}.

Precoding for per-subcarrier calibration. The precoding is performed on the input signal 𝐱\mathbf{x} to calibrate the non-flat frequency response of the channel. This is because 𝐱\mathbf{x} spans all the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} subcarriers, yet lacks any antenna-dimension information. Hereby, we define the precoder Ppre∈ℂNfftP_{\textrm{pre}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\textrm{fft}}}. Denoting the precoded signal by 𝐱′∈ℂNfft\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{\textrm{fft}}}, the precoding process can be expressed as a per-subcarrier multiplication between 𝐱\mathbf{x} and PpreP_{\textrm{pre}}:

(6) 𝐱′[k]=𝐱[k]⋅Ppre[k],∀k=0,1,…,Nfft−1.\displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{\prime}[k]=\mathbf{x}[k]\cdot P_{\textrm{pre}}[k],\quad\forall k=0,1,\ldots,N_{\textrm{fft}}-1.

Precoded linear convolution in analog. After the precoding, the input signal 𝐱′\mathbf{x}^{\prime} is split into AA ways and fed to the AA RF mixers, which perform the AA complex-valued convolutions in parallel against the respective received signals 𝐰a′\mathbf{w}^{\prime}_{a}, i.e.,

(7) 𝐲^a=𝐰′a⊤⋅𝐱′,∀a=0,1,…,A−1,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{a}={\mathbf{w}^{\prime}_{a}}^{\top}\cdot\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\quad\forall a=0,1,\ldots,A-1,

where 𝐲^a∈ℂ\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{a}\in\mathbb{C} is the unpostcoded output of antenna aa.

Postcoding for per-antenna calibration. The postcoding is performed on the output signal 𝐘\mathbf{Y} to calibrate the inter-antenna interference. This is because 𝐘\mathbf{Y} retains the full antenna dimension, while its frequency dimension is already down-sampled and aliased. Specifically, we define the postcoder Ppost∈ℂA×AP_{\textrm{post}}\in\mathbb{C}^{A\times A}, which is applied identically across all subcarriers; also, we denote the postcoded output signals by 𝐘^′={𝐲^a′}\widehat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\prime}=\{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime}_{a}\} with 𝐲^a′∈ℂ\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime}_{a}\in\mathbb{C}. (8) 𝐲^a′=∑a′=0A−1Ppost​[a,a′]⋅𝐲^a′.\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime}_{a}=\sum_{a^{\prime}=0}^{A-1}P_{\textrm{post}}[a,a^{\prime}]\cdot\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{a^{\prime}}.

Each calibration unit receives the same input signal 𝐱\mathbf{x} and the same received signals 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime} from the AA antennas, while applying a different precoder and postcoder, jointly denoted by Ppre∈ℂC×NfftP_{\textrm{pre}}\in\mathbb{C}^{C\times N_{\textrm{fft}}} and Ppost∈ℂC×A×AP_{\textrm{post}}\in\mathbb{C}^{C\times A\times A}. Finally, the outputs from all the calibration units are summed together into the final output, denoted by 𝐘^′′={𝐲^a′′}\widehat{\mathbf{Y}}^{\prime\prime}=\{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime\prime}_{a}\} with 𝐲^a′′∈ℂ\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime\prime}_{a}\in\mathbb{C}, i.e.,

3.3. Precoder and Postcoder Optimization

Putting (6), (7), (8), and (9) together, the ultimate goal of AIR-LLM is to minimize the mean squared error (MSE) between the final output signal 𝐲^′′\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime\prime} and the ground truth output signal 𝐲\mathbf{y} by optimizing the precoder PpreP_{\textrm{pre}} and postcoder PpostP_{\textrm{post}} jointly across all calibration units. We formulate this as the optimization problem in OPT-Orig.

OPT-Orig: Original precoder & postcoder optimization (10) Ppre⋆,Ppost⋆=arg⁡minPpre,Ppost​𝔼𝐱,𝐖​[∑a=0A−1‖𝐲^a′′−𝐲a‖22]\displaystyle P_{\textrm{pre}}^{\star},P_{\textrm{post}}^{\star}=\arg\min_{P_{\textrm{pre}},P_{\textrm{post}}}\ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{W}}\left[\sum_{a=0}^{A-1}\big\|\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime\prime}_{a}-\mathbf{y}_{a}\big\|_{2}^{2}\right]

Directly solving OPT-Orig requires the statistics of 𝐖\mathbf{W} and 𝐱\mathbf{x}. In practice, however, 𝐖\mathbf{W} and 𝐱\mathbf{x} are not known a priori at the edge device, and obtaining them would require an online training phase that feeds known instances of 𝐖\mathbf{W} and 𝐱\mathbf{x}. The overhead of such training is unaffordable, far exceeding the rate at which the channel HH itself varies over time.

Waiving the need of 𝐖\mathbf{W} and 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Fortunately, we observe that 𝐲^a′′−𝐲a\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\prime\prime}_{a}-\mathbf{y}_{a} is bilinear in (𝐖,𝐱)(\mathbf{W},\mathbf{x}), so the expectation objective in OPT-Orig depends only on the first/second-order statistics of 𝐖\mathbf{W} and 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Hence, we assume that the entries of 𝐖\mathbf{W} and 𝐱\mathbf{x} are zero-mean and mutually independent, and i.i.d. within each; we also assume a high SNR region that ignores the noise term in (1). Under these two assumptions, the second-order statistics of 𝐖\mathbf{W} and 𝐱\mathbf{x} reduce to scaled identity covariance matrices, so the expectation term in OPT-Orig collapses to a positive multiple of a channel-dependent-only objective, which becomes OPT-Chan below.

OPT-Chan: Simplified channel-dependent optimization (11) Ppre⋆,Ppost⋆=arg⁡minPpre,Ppost\displaystyle P_{\textrm{pre}}^{\star},P_{\textrm{post}}^{\star}=\arg\min_{P_{\textrm{pre}},P_{\textrm{post}}} (12) ∑k=0Nfft−1‖∑c=0C−1Ppre[c,k]⋅Ppost[c,:,:]⋅H[:,:,k]⊤−𝐈A‖2,\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{N_{\textrm{fft}}-1}\left\|\sum_{c=0}^{C-1}P_{\textrm{pre}}[c,k]\cdot P_{\textrm{post}}[c,:,:]\cdot{H[:,:,k]}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}_{A}\right\|^{2},

where 𝐈A\mathbf{I}_{A} is the A×AA\times A identity matrix. Intuitively, OPT-Chan requires the CC precoder-postcoder pairs to jointly zero-force every per-subcarrier channel matrix H[:,:,k]H[:,:,k] back to the identity matrix, independently of the weights 𝐖\mathbf{W} or inputs 𝐱\mathbf{x}. In the following, AIR-LLM solves OPT-Chan in two steps: initialization and fine-tuning.

Step 1: closed-form approximation for initialization. Generally, the objective in OPT-Chan is bilinear in PpreP_{\textrm{pre}} and PpostP_{\textrm{post}}, which jointly have to reproduce the inverse of the channel HH across all the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} subcarriers.

OPT-Approx: Approximation with closed-form solution (13) Ppre(0),P~post(0)=arg⁡minP~post,Ppre⁡‖P~post⋅Ppre−H~−1‖2.\displaystyle P_{\textrm{pre}}^{(0)},\tilde{P}_{\textrm{post}}^{(0)}=\arg\min_{\tilde{P}_{\textrm{post}},P_{\textrm{pre}}}\left\|\tilde{P}_{\textrm{post}}\cdot P_{\textrm{pre}}-\tilde{H}^{-1}\right\|^{2}.

Relative to OPT-Chan, OPT-Approx introduces a single approximation: it drops the inherent per-subcarrier weighting by the channel magnitudes, as the residual in OPT-Chan is exactly that of OPT-Approx right-multiplied by H[:,:,k]⊤{H[:,:,k]}^{\top}. Specifically, (⋅~)(\tilde{\cdot}) denotes merging the two antenna dimensions into one, so that OPT-Approx introduces the flattened postcoder P~post∈ℂA2×C\tilde{P}_{\textrm{post}}\in\mathbb{C}^{A^{2}\times C} and the flattened channel inverse H~−1∈ℂA2×Nfft\tilde{H}^{-1}\in\mathbb{C}^{A^{2}\times N_{\textrm{fft}}}, the latter inverted per subcarrier. By the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem (Mirsky, 1960), OPT-Approx can be solved in closed form by taking the singular value decomposition (SVD) of H~−1\tilde{H}^{-1} and keeping its CC largest singular values. Unflattening the resulting P~post(0)\tilde{P}_{\textrm{post}}^{(0)} back into the two antenna dimensions provides the initialization of OPT-Chan, denoted by Ppre(0)P_{\textrm{pre}}^{(0)} and Ppost(0)P_{\textrm{post}}^{(0)}.

Step 2: alternating least squares (ALS) for fine-tuning. Starting from Ppre(0)P_{\textrm{pre}}^{(0)} and Ppost(0)P_{\textrm{post}}^{(0)}, we refine towards the objective in OPT-Chan by alternating between two convex and closed-form least-squares updates until convergence:

  • • Precoder step: fixing PpostP_{\textrm{post}}, we optimize PpreP_{\textrm{pre}} to balance the zero-forcing residual across the frequency dimension, i.e., the NfftN_{\textrm{fft}} subcarriers, which reduces to a linear least-squares problem solved independently per subcarrier.
  • • Postcoder step: fixing PpreP_{\textrm{pre}}, we optimize PpostP_{\textrm{post}} to cancel the inter-antenna interference respectively for each subcarrier, which also reduces to a linear least-squares problem, solved independently per output antenna.

Both steps admit closed-form solutions, so each ALS iteration is cheap; given the Step 1 initialization, convergence typically occurs within a handful of iterations. A detailed optimization process of these two steps is shown in Appendix B.2 and B.3.

3.4. System Efficiency Analysis

We analyze the efficiency of AIR-LLM along two dimensions: the airtime it occupies the wireless channel, and the energy it consumes on the edge device.

Airtime analysis. The airtime of AIR-LLM is inversely proportional to the number of antennas AA and the occupied bandwidth BB. Interestingly, this form exactly follows a conventional communication link with spatial multiplexing on AA and frequency multiplexing on BB. On the other hand, AIR-LLM’s airtime is independent of the SNR, which instead determines the computing accuracy; AIR-LLM therefore does not customize the transmitted signals for each user, and is naturally fit to broadcasting. Leveraged by broadcasting, one transmission of the weights serves arbitrarily many edge users at a constant airtime, so the airtime amortized per user decreases as 1/U1/U. The complete analysis is given in Appendix C.3.

Energy analysis. Overall, AIR-LLM achieves good energy efficiency on RF computing, whose energy per FLOP is further averaged down as the GEMV scales up to LLM. This is because the energy consumption of almost every hardware component in AIR-LLM is amortized by either the input size NN or the output size MM, leaving the DAC, whose per-FLOP energy is set by the antenna number AA and the unit number CC, as the floor that a large GEMV converges to. Such a scaling law is contributed by two key designs. First, the RF mixer and the LPF collapse the whole input dimension into a single subcarrier with a downsampling ratio of NN, so the ADC takes only one sample per inner product, which usually dominates the energy budget of an analog computing system; the postcoding runs on that same single sample per antenna, so its energy is amortized by NN as well. Second, the precoding and the IFFT are paid only once per GEMV, as the same precoded input signal 𝐱′\mathbf{x}^{\prime} is reused across all the ⌈M/(2​A)⌉\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil rounds, so their energy is amortized by the output size MM. The per-component analysis is in Appendix C.4.

Tradeoff on computing accuracy, airtime, and energy. The calibration unit number CC is where these three metrics meet. On the accuracy side, OPT-Chan calibrates the channel with a rank-CC approximation, so a larger CC leaves a smaller residual and thus a more accurate channel calibration; and the more antennas AA are deployed, the larger CC this accuracy requires. On the energy side, however, every energy term grows linearly with CC. Scaling up AA therefore shortens the airtime but pays for its accuracy in energy, so CC should be the smallest that meets the target task’s accuracy.

4. 执行

We implement AIR-LLM on the wireless channels of real-world urban scenes by a ray-tracing simulator, and on the distortion of a real RF mixer, measured on a wired testbed.

4.1. Channel Modeling by Ray Tracing

Sionna ray-tracing simulator. We build the wireless channel between the central radio and the edge devices on top of NVIDIA Sionna’s ray-tracing engine (v2.0.1) (Hoydis et al., 2022; Hoydis et al., 2023). Specifically, Sionna simulates the wireless signal propagation process by shooting 10710^{7} rays into a digital twin of a real-world city scene and resolving their interactions (e.g., reflection, refraction, and diffraction) with the buildings, grounds, etc. Assembling these propagation paths, it provides the realistic channel HH that the weight signal 𝐖\mathbf{W} propagates through to each of the edge devices. As shown in Fig. 4(a) and (b), we evaluate AIR-LLM in two contrasting urban scenes: (i) Place Charles de Gaulle in Paris, open enough that a line-of-sight (LOS) path always holds, and (ii) the city center of Munich, densely built so that multipath is rich while the LOS path is often blocked.

Central radio configuration. The central radio sits at the center of each scene, 10 m above the ground. It carries AA antennas (A=4A=4 by default) on ⌈A/2⌉\left\lceil{A/2}\right\rceil physical elements, each of two orthogonal polarizations, spaced 1.7 m apart. It broadcasts the weight signal on the CBRS band (Sohul et al., 2015) at a 3.5 GHz carrier frequency over 100 MHz of bandwidth. The default broadcast power per antenna is set to 50 dBm, and the coverage radius is 100 m.

Edge device configuration. We randomly drop 100 edge devices at 1.5 m height within the central radio’s coverage zone. Each edge device carries the same cross-polarized AA-port array with 4.3 cm spacing (half-wavelength), and C=8C=8 calibration units, whose coders are derived from a least-squares per-antenna pilot estimate H^\widehat{H}. We assume the devices’ noise figure of 4 dB, corresponding to a noise floor of -90 dBm across the 100 MHz bandwidth; their path loss (PL) from the central radio is estimated by its own channel as −10​log10⁡(𝔼⁡[|H|2])-10\log_{10}(\mathbb{E}[|H|^{2}]).

4.2. Hardware Profiling on Real RF Mixer

RF mixers are not built for analog multiplication, and hence distort the desired product. We therefore measure the distortion of a real RF mixer, ZEM-4300+ (Mini-Circuits, 2024), driven by USRP X310 radios (Ettus Research, 2024) as the transceivers, as shown in Fig. 4(c). The profiling is wired, so the power entering the mixer stays far above the noise floor; the link is thus considered noiseless, and the computing errors are fully attributed to the mixer’s own distortion. Specifically, for each power at the mixer’s RF port, which receives the weight signal over the air in a deployment, we sweep the power at its LO port and keep the lowest distortion error, i.e., the best effective number of bits (ENOB), that the mixer reaches. The measured distortion ENOB curve over the RF power is shown in Fig. A2 of Appendix E.1. In our evaluation, we read this curve at each edge device’s received weight signal power and plug in the corresponding distortion error.
