5.1. Benchmarking on GEMV

We first benchmark AIR-LLM on a single GEMV with randomized weights and input activations. The computing accuracy is measured by ENOB defined in Appendix E.3.

GEMV accuracy over the user PL. Following the default setup in §4.1, Fig. 5 scatters the ENOB of a randomized GEMV by each of the 100 candidate users in Paris and Munich against their PLs. The ENOB generally decreases with the PL, as a higher PL lowers the power, and thus the SNR, of the weight signal arriving at the user. The open scene of Paris, where an LOS path is more likely and the PL is therefore lower (median 84.0 dB), reaches a median ENOB of 3.97 bit with 5/95-th percentiles of 1.58/5.69 bit, whereas the users of Munich, mostly without an LOS path (median 91.4 dB), reach only 2.91 bit with 0.53/5.33 bit. In addition, the PL does not determine the ENOB, which further depends on how the received power is spread over the multi-path components: within a PL of 89–91 dB alone, the ENOB still ranges over 2.01–5.33 bit. We empirically select the user with approximately 4.00 bit at 86.3 dB in Paris and that of approximately 3.00 bit at 94.1 dB in Munich, starred in the figure, as the default for the experiments below.

GEMV accuracy over the central radio power. Fig. 5 sweeps the central radio transmit power from 30 dBm to 70 dBm on the two selected users. Both scenes follow the same two-stage trend: the ENOB first grows by roughly 1 bit per 10 dB of transmit power, and then saturates. The Munich user, for example, climbs from 1.20 bit at 30 dBm to 3.55 bit at 55 dBm, but to only 3.87 bit when further increased to 70 dBm power. In the first stage, the GEMV accuracy is limited by the received weight signal power against the noise floor; in the second, by the imperfect channel compensation of the CC units and the RF mixer’s imperfect multiplication.

Trading off computing accuracy, energy, and airtime. Compared to WISE (Gao et al., 2026b), the special case of AIR-LLM with A=C=1A=C=1, AIR-LLM involves MIMO to save the airtime of a GEMV: the airtime is proportional to the inverse antenna number 1/A1/A. On the other hand, the corresponding wireless channel takes more calibration units CC to compensate, and the energy consumption is proportional to CC. Fig. 6 illustrates this trade-off in Paris on a single-round GEMV of M=2​AM=2A and N=4,096N={4,096}, sweeping C={1,2,…,A2}C=\left\{1,2,\dots,A^{2}\right\} at A={2,4,8,16,32}A=\left\{2,4,8,16,32\right\}, i.e., an airtime gain of 2/4/8/16/32×\times over WISE, with each array at the central radio power of 40/50/60/70/80 dBm. Given AA, a larger CC compensates for the channel more accurately and is saturated at some point depending on the channel’s complexity. At A=4A={4}, for example, the ENOB climbs from 0.55 bit at C=1C={1} to 3.97 at 8 units and 5.07 at 10; five further units then add only 0.43 bit while costing 1.5×\times the energy. Fig. 6 extracts the minimum energy reaching each ENOB level, normalized to that by WISE: 3 bit costs 1.02/1.90/3.86/5.09/9.60×\times and 4 bit costs 1.54/2.44/5.86/6.96/13.59×\times at A=2/4/8/16/32A={2/4/8/16/32}. This suggests that, to reduce the airtime with a larger AA, the same ENOB requires more energy consumption, because an A2A^{2}-entry per-subcarrier matrix takes more units to invert. The same trends hold in Munich, whose results are shown in Appendix F.1.

Scaling up the GEMV size. In Fig. 7, we scale up the GEMV’s input and output sizes together, over N=M={20,21,…,214}N=M=\left\{2^{0},2^{1},\dots,2^{14}\right\}. Up to N=M=23N=M=2^{3}, where a GEMV is completed within a single round, the computing accuracy stays at 5.58–5.75 bit in Paris and 3.85–3.94 bit in Munich. Beyond that point, where multiple rounds are needed, the ENOB drops slightly to 3.99–4.51 and 3.10–3.39 bit, respectively, which is maintained as the size keeps scaling up. AIR-LLM therefore supports good computing accuracy on the large-scale GEMVs that are widely used in LLMs. Fig. 7 further illustrates the energy per FLOP over the same sweep of GEMV scales, normalized to that of the FP16 baseline. That of FP16 and of the WoQ baselines, counting both the data movement and the digital computing, is constant over the sweep, with W4A16/W3A16 3.72/4.80×\times more energy efficient than FP16. In contrast, AIR-LLM’s energy per FLOP scales down as the GEMV scales up. A small GEMV is bottlenecked by the digital arithmetic of the precoding, the IFFT, and the postcoding (e.g., only 3.81×\times more energy efficient than FP16 at N=24N=2^{4}), after which the bottleneck moves to the DAC, whose per-FLOP cost is constant over the GEMV size (e.g., 50.2×\times more energy efficient than FP16 at N=212N=2^{12}). The ADC energy, which dominates conventional analog computing, is nearly free because of AIR-LLM’s downsampling ratio of NN. In applications whose GEMV input is itself an analog waveform, e.g., a received wireless signal or a biomedical sensor readout, this bottlenecked DAC energy is waived as well. This is exactly the regime an LLM runs in, whose inference is dominated by large GEMVs, and where AIR-LLM therefore costs the edge device the least.

5.2. Benchmarking on LLM

We run whole LLMs with all weight-activation GEMVs computed in analog by AIR-LLM, and the remaining in digital. The LLM tasks and the WoQ/analog computing baselines are described in Appendix E.2 and E.3.

PPL on WikiText-2. In Tab. 2, we present the WikiText-2 PPL at the sequence length of 2,048 over nine LLMs of four families: LLaMA-3.2 (1B and 3B), LLaMA-3.1 (8B and 70B), LLaMA-2 (7B and 13B), Mistral-7B, and Gemma-4 (E2B and E4B). The selected user in Paris, resolving about 4 bit, is read against the W4A16 baselines (RTN, GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023), and AWQ (Lin et al., 2024)) and the ENOB-4 analog computing baselines (AWGN and HyFlexPIM (Song et al., 2025)); the user in Munich, at about 3 bit, against their W3A16 and ENOB-3 counterparts. In Paris, specifically, AIR-LLM beats the best of the WoQ baselines on 7 out of the 9 LLMs, and the best of the analog computing baselines on 4 of the 9, staying within 5.6% of it on the other five. In Munich, where every baseline loses more at 3 bit, it beats the best of the W3A16 and of the ENOB-3 baselines on 7 and 5 of the 9, respectively. Such comparable or slightly lower PPLs show that the errors of AIR-LLM, including the thermal noise, the hardware distortion, and the imperfect channel compensation, still leave enough computing accuracy for an LLM inference.

Energy consumption per token. Fig. 8 illustrates the per-token energy the edge device spends on the nine LLMs at the selected user in Paris, against four baselines that combine the remote/local weight storage with the FP16/W4A16 precision. All these energy consumptions are normalized to that of the remote FP16 on LLaMA-3.1-8B. On the same LLaMA-3.1-8B, AIR-LLM costs 157.7×\times and 40.4×\times less energy than the remote FP16 and W4A16, respectively, and against the local FP16 and W4A16, whose weights are more easily accessible from the device’s own memory, AIR-LLM still wins by 51.5×\times and 13.9×\times. Such an energy gain holds over all nine LLMs. Specifically for the two W4A16 baselines, whose PPL is comparable to AIR-LLM, AIR-LLM gains 35.4–44.0×\times against the remote one, owing to the downsampling ratio of NN at AIR-LLM’s ADC, as well as the much lighter digital pipeline behind it. AIR-LLM even achieves 12.9–14.3×\times against the local one, whose weights are easier to access than AIR-LLM’s, thanks to the waiving of the energy-expensive data movement. The Munich device draws the same conclusion against its own W3A16 baselines, as reported in Fig. A5.

Airtime per token. In Paris, Fig. 9 presents the per-token airtime occupying the wireless channel, including AIR-LLM and the two remote baselines on the same nine LLMs. Similarly, the airtime is normalized to that of the remote FP16 on LLaMA-3.1-8B; the two local baselines occupy no channel and are therefore skipped. On LLaMA-3.1-8B, AIR-LLM takes 5.11×\times less airtime than the remote FP16 baseline, and slightly less airtime of 1.28×\times compared to the W4A16 baseline. Both ratios stay constant at 5.11×\times and 1.28×\times across all nine LLMs, as the airtime of AIR-LLM and that of the remote baselines are proportional to the same weight count. In this single-user case, the close airtime to the W4A16 baseline comes from the physical limit of the wireless channel (27): the airtime is scaled down linearly with the bandwidth BB and the antenna number AA for both the communication and AIR-LLM’s computing, and their remaining difference in the SNR is canceled out once the baseline is quantized to the specific weight width giving the close PPL performance to AIR-LLM. Similar ratios are also observed in Munich in Fig. A5 of Appendix F.2. In a dense-user scenario, however, AIR-LLM’s broadcasting capability significantly outperforms these WoQ baselines regarding the airtime, which is later shown in §5.4.

PPL over the sequence length. In Tab. 3, we sweep the sequence length from 256 to 16,384 tokens to evaluate AIR-LLM’s robustness over the context length of the prefilling phase. The PPLs of the FP16 baseline and of AIR-LLM in Paris/Munich fall as the context grows, and AIR-LLM’s relative gap to the FP16 reference narrows and then flattens, spanning 3.9–6.6% and 17.1–25.3% over the sweep while settling at about 4.0% and 17.3% beyond 2,048 tokens. This suggests that AIR-LLM’s computing error does not accumulate along the context, and that the same robustness would potentially extend to the much longer contexts demanded by future LLM applications. Note that AIR-LLM’s per-token energy and airtime are constant along this axis, since both are dominated by streaming the weights of each layer once per token, independent of the token number.

5.3. Impact of the System Factors

We examine more deployment factors, such as transmit power, antenna/calibration unit number, and frequency band.

Impact of the central radio transmit power. We evaluate the impact of the transmit power under the same LLaMA-3.1-8B setup in Paris and Munich, which is presented in Tab. 4. The Paris user is already saturated at 35 dBm with 9.1% above the FP16 reference of 6.24, and raising the power to 60 dBm narrows that gap only to 3.8%. This hints that the computing error of this user comes from the imprecise channel calibration and the RF mixer’s imperfection. In comparison, the Munich user is still power-limited: its PPL stays orders of magnitude above the FP16 reference below 50 dBm, and then improves steeply to 8.8% at 60 dBm, meaning that its computing accuracy is mainly determined by the thermal noise. Both observations match the two-stage trend of Fig. 5. In AIR-LLM, users under different channel conditions are limited by different sources of the computing error, which in turn decides whether more transmit power pays off.

Impact of the antenna and calibration unit number. The joint impact of AA and CC on LLaMA-3.1-8B’s PPL is shown in Tab. 5, where we consider A={4,8}A=\left\{4,8\right\} with different CC. Given A=4A={4}, the PPL falls from above 10510^{5} at 2 units to 6.49/7.37 at 8 units in Paris/Munich and then saturates; as for A=8A={8}, the saturation point moves to around 32 units, with 6.74/6.95 PPLs, respectively. Theoretically, a perfect inversion takes C=A2C=A^{2} units in OPT-Approx; in practice, fortunately, approximately A2/2A^{2}/2 units already achieve a good PPL on LLM applications, saving approximately 1/2 energy consumption. This is because a realistic channel comprises a limited number of multi-path components, whose singular values decay rapidly.

Performance in other bands. We repeat the sweeps above in the 0.915 GHz ISM band with 25 MHz bandwidth, and the 28 GHz mmWave band with 400 MHz bandwidth, on the same two users in Paris/Munich, as summarized in Tab. 6. Moving the frequency changes both the PL and the richness of the multipath; the former is compensated by setting its own broadcast power. The PPLs at 0.915 GHz are accordingly comparable to those at 3.5 GHz, within 0.42 of each other across the eight (A,C)(A,C) combinations, whereas the sparser multipath at 28 GHz leaves the Munich user unusable, with PPLs always >102>10^{2} even at 90 dBm. The full results can be found in Appendix F.3.

5.4. Broadcasting to Massive Edge Users

Finally, we move to the 20-edge-user scenes served by a single central radio’s broadcasting LLM weights.

PPL over the edge users. Fig. 10 marks the positions of the 20 edge users per scene, spanning PLs of 70.0–99.9 dB in Paris and 68.6–105.0 dB in Munich. We also label each user with its respective PPL on LLaMA-3.1-8B using AIR-LLM, and the CDFs are further given in Fig. 11. Specifically for Paris, the median PPL is 6.52, better than the W4A16 baseline of 6.65, and in Munich it is 7.23, better than the W3A16 baseline of 8.24; 70% and 80% of the users, respectively, fall below these two baselines. Note that one extreme user in Paris suffers an outlier PPL of 255.27. Despite its PL of 84.0 dB, its received power concentrates on too few multi-path components to support spatial multiplexing, which leaves its channel matrix HH nearly singular. Such a degradation also appears for the communication-based baselines whose channel capacity collapses on the same link; for AIR-LLM, it can be alleviated by falling back to fewer antennas AA, which trades the airtime for a better-conditioned HH.

Energy over the edge users. The averaged per-token energy of AIR-LLM over the same set of 20 users against the four baselines of each scene is shown in Fig. 11. In Paris, AIR-LLM consumes 160.5×\times/41.1×\times less mean energy than the remote FP16 and W4A16 baselines, and 51.5×\times/13.9×\times less than the two local ones; similar numbers of 160.6×\times/31.2×\times and 51.5×\times/10.7×\times can also be observed in Munich comparing to the W3A16 baselines. AIR-LLM’s energy consumption is constant regardless of users’ positions and wireless channels, and is stably better than both the communication-based remote baselines, whose energy follows each user’s own link, and the data movement-based local ones.

Airtime over the edge users. Fig. 12 plots the total airtime that one token takes while the first UU users are served. The communication baselines are based on unicasting, where every user is served separately at its own MCS customized to its channel quality. Thus, serving UU users costs U×U\times the airtime of a single user, and the total grows linearly. In comparison, AIR-LLM broadcasts the weights for the 20 users simultaneously, because the central radio is user-unaware and one uniform transmission is fed to every user inside the coverage. Therefore, the airtime of AIR-LLM is constant over UU, which is 104.1×\times/26.0×\times less than that by the FP16/W4A16 baselines with 20 users. Munich shows the same in Fig. A7 of Appendix F.4. This broadcast- and user-scalable feature lets AIR-LLM serve the thriving number of future edge users.

6. Related Works

LLM accelerators. Serving an LLM is memory-bounded by the weight movement rather than arithmetic (Guo et al., 2025). One category of works shrinks the bits per weight and co-designs the compute units around the resulting mixed-format GEMVs (Frantar et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2023; Tseng et al., 2024), with the hardware absorbing the outliers (Guo et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024) or the dequantization (Park et al., 2025; Mo et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026); a second attacks the movement rather than the format, placing the compute next to the memory that holds the weights and the KV cache (Park et al., 2024; Heo et al., 2024; Yun et al., 2024). All share one premise: the weights are already stored in the device’s memory, and only the cost of fetching and multiplying a resident weight is optimized. AIR-LLM removes that premise: no weight is stored on the edge device; each arrival of the broadcast weight waveform is consumed and computed directly in the RF/analog domain.

Analog computing for ML inference. Analog computing performs the FLOPs in physics rather than in digital, escaping the energy floor of digital arithmetic: in-memory computing completes a GEMV on a ReRAM, PCM, or SRAM crossbar through Ohm’s and Kirchhoff’s laws (Shafiee et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2022; Le Gallo et al., 2023), while photonic computing multiplies operands encoded onto light (Shen et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2023). However, such designs are usually limited by their analog error and readout converters (Zhang et al., 2025; Khaddam-Aljameh et al., 2022), yet already carry real models at a handful of effective bits (Ambrogio et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024); AIR-LLM likewise reports every result at the effective bits its link resolves (Dettmers and Zettlemoyer, 2023). Closest in spirit is the work that lets operand delivery and computation happen in the same physical layer, over fiber (Sludds et al., 2022) or over the air (Reus-Muns et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2026b; Gao et al., 2026a), the latter inside a commodity receiver’s RF mixer; unlike over-the-air computation, which superposes many transmitters into a sum (Nazer and Gastpar, 2007; Zhu et al., 2020), AIR-LLM’s mixer forms a product of an arriving weight waveform with a local input. In addition, AIR-LLM generalizes the single-antenna and single-weight-stream into an A×AA\times A MIMO engine to largely reduce the airtime, whose calibration units zero-force a real, frequency-selective channel.

LLM deployment on the edge. On-device LLM serving is a capacity problem before a compute one, and the systems response keeps as few weights resident as possible: pruning (Niu et al., 2020), activation sparsity (Song et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024), flash streaming (Alizadeh et al., 2024), or accelerator–model co-design (Yu et al., 2024). Yet even a quantized resident model stays memory-bound on commodity phones, where energy and thermals make continuous generation untenable (Laskaridis et al., 2024). The complementary response moves the model off the device (Kwon et al., 2023; Stojkovic et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2017), trading the memory wall for a per-query network cost and for handing the prompt to the server. Both leave each device paying, privately and per token, for the same weights that every other device in the cell also pays for (Qu et al., 2024). AIR-LLM instead disaggregates the weight storage to the central radio while keeping both the computation and the prompt on the edge, and because its transmission is edge-device-unaware, one broadcast is mixed by every device in the coverage at once, amortizing the delivery cost over the devices served. Such one-to-many analog delivery has precedent in SoftCast (Jakubczak and Katabi, 2011), which broadcasts video over raw OFDM at a fidelity set by each receiver’s own channel.

7. 结论

In this paper, we present AIR-LLM, an LLM inference architecture for edge users that is memory-access-free, user-scalable and energy-efficient. Specifically, AIR-LLM exploits MIMO spatial multiplexing to deliver multiple weight streams at a time and thereby shorten the airtime, and the design of the precoder–postcoder pair on the edge user energy-efficiently calibrates its own wireless channel. Exhaustive evaluations on the NVIDIA Sionna ray-traced channels and the profiling of a real RF mixer reveal that, with a slight PPL gap to the FP16 baseline, AIR-LLM cuts the per-token energy and airtime by orders of magnitude. We believe AIR-LLM opens up a new path for the next generation of edge intelligence.

Appendix B Blocked Correlation Operation

We generalize the linear-convolution mapping into a blocked correlation operation (BCO), where the mixer retains a whole output block of subcarriers rather than a single one.

B.1. Definition and Realization

Definition of BCO. We define the BCO by ⋆\star. Its two operands, weights and inputs, are both complex valued, given by 𝐰∈ℂD×Lw\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{C}^{D\times L_{w}} and 𝐱∈ℂD×Lx\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{D\times L_{x}}, each consisting of DD blocks. These DD blocks are correlated in parallel, and their correlation outputs are accumulated into a single output block 𝐲∈ℂL\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{C}^{L}, defined as

𝐲⁡[k]\displaystyle\mathbf{y}[k] =(𝐰⋆𝐱)​[k]\displaystyle=\left(\mathbf{w}\star\mathbf{x}\right)[k]
(14) =∑d=0D−1∑k′=max⁡(0,k−Lx+1)min⁡(k,Lw−1)𝐰⁡[d,k′]⋅𝐱⁡[d,k′−k+Lx−1],\displaystyle=\sum_{d=0}^{D-1}\sum_{k^{\prime}=\max(0,\,k-L_{x}+1)}^{\min(k,\,L_{w}-1)}\mathbf{w}[d,k^{\prime}]\cdot\mathbf{x}[d,k^{\prime}-k+L_{x}-1],

where the block sizes satisfy L=Lw+Lx−1L=L_{w}+L_{x}-1. A BCO thus costs D​Lw​LxDL_{w}L_{x} additions and as many multiplications, i.e., 2​D​Lw​Lx2DL_{w}L_{x} FLOPs. The GEMV mapping of (4) is the degenerate case D=ND=N and Lw=Lx=L=1L_{w}=L_{x}=L=1, in which every block holds one scalar and (14) reduces to the NN-element inner product of (5).

Realizing BCO with an RF mixer. In the frequency domain, an RF mixer convolves two analog signals, WW and XX, into YY, which is the correlation of (14) once one operand is reversed in subcarrier order, as in (4). To realize a BCO, we let the FFT size be Nfft=D⋅LN_{\textrm{fft}}=D\cdot L, i.e., one length-LL subcarrier slot per block. The frequency-domain weight signal W∈ℂD​LW\in\mathbb{C}^{DL} is obtained from 𝐰\mathbf{w} by zero-padding each block 𝐰[d,:]\mathbf{w}[d,:] into the length-LL segment W[dL:(d+1)L−1]W[dL:(d+1)L-1], and the input signal X∈ℂD​LX\in\mathbb{C}^{DL} is obtained from 𝐱\mathbf{x} in the same way, i.e.,

(15) W⁡[d​L+k]\displaystyle W[dL+k] ={𝐰⁡[d,k],k<Lw,0,k≥Lw,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathbf{w}[d,k],&k<L_{w},\\ 0,&k\geq L_{w},\end{cases}
X⁡[d​L+k]\displaystyle X[dL+k] ={𝐱⁡[d,k],k<Lx,0,k≥Lx,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathbf{x}[d,k],&k<L_{x},\\ 0,&k\geq L_{x},\end{cases}

for all d=0,1,…,D−1d=0,1,\dots,D-1 and k=0,1,…,L−1k=0,1,\dots,L-1. The zero padding guarantees that the correlation of one block never leaks into the subcarrier slot of the next. Correlating WW with XX spans 2​D−12D-1 slots, and every matching block pair (d,d)(d,d) lands in the same, middle slot of index D−1D-1, which therefore accumulates the correlation outputs of all DD blocks, exactly as (14) prescribes. This middle slot is extracted by the LPF, whose output signal Y∈ℂLY\in\mathbb{C}^{L} satisfies Y⁡[k]=𝐲⁡[k]Y[k]=\mathbf{y}[k] for all k=0,1,…,L−1k=0,1,\dots,L-1. Since the subcarrier spacing Δ​f\Delta f is shared by all three signals, this output occupies a bandwidth of only B/DB/D and is digitized with D×D\times fewer ADC samples than the full-band signal, which is where AIR-LLM’s ADC energy saving comes from.

Implication on the calibration units. The calibration unit of §3.3 carries over unchanged, with one structural caveat on the precoder. Under BCO, the LL subcarriers within a block jointly carry one correlation, so they must be scaled identically: a per-subcarrier precoder would reweight the individual correlation taps and destroy the block structure of (14). The precoder is therefore constant within each block, i.e., Ppre∈ℂC×DP_{\textrm{pre}}\in\mathbb{C}^{C\times D} with the subcarrier kk driven by Ppre​[c,⌊k/L⌋]P_{\textrm{pre}}[c,\left\lfloor{k/L}\right\rfloor], which is precisely the form optimized in (17) of §B.2. The postcoder, in contrast, acts across antennas only and is applied identically to all subcarriers, so it is unaffected. For a GEMV, L=1L=1 makes the per-block and the per-subcarrier precoder identical, recovering the main-body design.

B.2. Pre-/Post-coder Optimization

Following the optimization derivation in §3.3, the BCO version of the optimization can be written as

B.3. Convergence of the Optimization

We study how the two-step solve converges on the GEMV, i.e., the degenerate case L=1L=1 in which (17) reduces to the OPT-Chan of §3.3. The two edge devices are the selected users of Paris and Munich of §5.1, resolving approximately 4.00 and 3.00 bit, so the numbers below are directly comparable to the evaluation.

What each step buys. Fig. A1 traces the two steps on the selected edge device of each scene. Before either of them, the raw link is unusable: fitting the single complex gain that an AGC and a carrier recovery already provide leaves 0.00 bit in Paris and 0.05 bit in Munich, i.e., the frequency selectivity of HH and its inter-antenna mixing alone destroy the GEMV. The closed-form Step-1 initialization recovers most of it at once, cutting the loss of (17) from 0.998 to 0.013 in Paris and from 0.947 to 0.259 in Munich, i.e., to 3.12 and 0.97 bit. The gap between the two scenes is the price of the per-block channel approximation of (19): the richer multipath of Munich makes the frequency response vary within a block, so the averaged H¯\bar{H} that Step 1 inverts sits further from the per-subcarrier channel that (17) actually scores, and the SVD initialization alone is worth about one bit there against three in Paris.

How many ALS iterations. Figs. A1 and A1 answer how long Step 2 has to run. A single ALS pass recovers most of what Step 1 leaves behind, dropping the loss by a further 2.7×\times in Paris and 17.5×\times in Munich to reach 3.79 and 2.85 bit. Everything after that pass is a slow creep: iterations 2 through 10 add only 0.13 bit in Paris and 0.29 bit in Munich, and the relative-tolerance test stops the two devices at 40 and 22 iterations, at 4.08 and 3.13 bit. Since one iteration is two closed-form least-squares solves and the optimization runs once per channel coherence time rather than per GEMV, we run it to that convergence throughout the evaluation, though stopping after the first pass would already sit within 0.29 bit of it.

Appendix C Airtime and Energy Consumption

This section analyzes the two efficiency metrics of AIR-LLM, the airtime and the energy consumption per FLOP. We derive them at the general block size of a BCO (§C.1 and §C.2), and then substitute the GEMV mapping of the main body, its degenerate case, to read off the airtime and the energy of a GEMV (§C.3 and §C.4).

C.1. Airtime of a BCO

We analyze the airtime of AIR-LLM, i.e., how long the RF chain of an edge device is occupied to compute one FLOP. It is bottlenecked by the duration of the signals, both the wireless one carrying 𝐖\mathbf{W} from the central radio and the local one carrying 𝐱\mathbf{x}, which the bandwidth BB sets.

Airtime per round. Each round of AIR-LLM receives one OFDM symbol carrying 𝐖\mathbf{W} across the Nfft=D​LN_{\textrm{fft}}=DL subcarriers, feeding AA antennas/RF mixers for 2​A2A parallel BCOs, two of them packed per antenna into the real and the imaginary parts; a layer of MM outputs, all sharing the same input 𝐱\mathbf{x}, thus takes ⌈M/(2​A)⌉\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil rounds. The airtime per round then scales as

(23) T∝D​LB.\displaystyle T\propto\frac{DL}{B}.

Airtime per FLOP. Normalizing (23) by the FLOPs that the 2​A2A parallel BCOs complete within the round gives the per-FLOP airtime of a general BCO,

(24) τ∝LA​B​Lw​Lx.\displaystyle\tau\propto\frac{L}{ABL_{w}L_{x}}.

The block number DD cancels out: splitting a layer into more, smaller blocks lengthens the round and adds FLOPs in the same proportion. More generally, (24) rewards a block layout whose output block is short relative to the product of the two input block sizes, i.e., one whose correlation reuses each transmitted weight over many taps.

C.2. Energy Consumption of a BCO

We analyze the edge-device-side energy consumption of AIR-LLM per FLOP by its complexity, i.e., the number of operations on three kinds of hardware, each costing a constant energy per operation: the DAC and the ADC, counted in samples, and the digital computing, counted in FLOPs.

Energy per module. We account for the energy of one whole module, i.e., all ⌈M/(2​A)⌉\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil rounds of 2​A2A BCOs, and then normalize by the FLOPs it completes, breaking the module energy into seven components along the signal chain,

(25) E=Epre+Eifft+Edac+Eadc+Efft+Epost+Esum,\displaystyle E=E_{\textrm{pre}}+E_{\textrm{ifft}}+E_{\textrm{dac}}+E_{\textrm{adc}}+E_{\textrm{fft}}+E_{\textrm{post}}+E_{\textrm{sum}},

i.e., the precoding, the IFFT, the DAC, the ADC, the FFT, the postcoding, and the cross-unit summation. Each of the CC calibration units precodes 𝐱\mathbf{x} per block and takes an NfftN_{\textrm{fft}}-point IFFT. Both are paid only once for the whole module: PpreP_{\textrm{pre}} depends solely on the channel and every round mixes the same 𝐱\mathbf{x} with a new set of broadcast weights, so the precoded waveform is buffered and replayed across the rounds. Within each of the ⌈M/(2​A)⌉≈M/(2​A)\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil\approx M/(2A) rounds, every unit then converts the waveform with one DAC over Nfft=D​LN_{\textrm{fft}}=DL samples, digitizes the LPF output of LL samples per antenna, and decodes it with a LL-point FFT plus postcoding, before the CC units are summed. Accumulating the latter five over the rounds gives the “Energy per module” column of Tab. A3, and dividing each term by the 2​M​D​Lw​Lx2MDL_{w}L_{x} FLOPs of the module gives its “Energy per FLOP” column. Note that the ADC term is charged for LL samples rather than NfftN_{\textrm{fft}}, since the BCO output occupies only the reduced bandwidth B/DB/D.

Unlike the airtime of (24), the block number DD does not cancel here: it amortizes the receiver-side terms while it stretches the IFFT logarithmically, which is the trade-off a concrete block layout has to settle.

C.3. Airtime of a GEMV

Airtime per GEMV. Under the GEMV mapping, D=ND=N and Lw=Lx=L=1L_{w}=L_{x}=L=1, so that Nfft=NN_{\textrm{fft}}=N and each round of (23) produces 2​A2A IPs. A GEMV of MM IPs therefore takes ⌈M/(2​A)⌉\left\lceil{M/(2A)}\right\rceil such rounds in serial, i.e., a signal duration per GEMV of

(26) T∝M​NA​B.\displaystyle T\propto\frac{MN}{AB}.

Airtime per FLOP. Within this duration, AIR-LLM completes the entire GEMV of M⁡(2​N−1)M(2N-1) FLOPs, so that

(27) τ∝1A​B,\displaystyle\tau\propto\frac{1}{AB},

which is (24) at unit block sizes.

Airtime scaling law. Notably, both layer sizes NN and MM cancel out of (27): a larger GEMV proportionally stretches the signal duration and the number of FLOPs completed within it, leaving the per-FLOP airtime unchanged. What remains is governed solely by the bandwidth BB and the antenna number AA, independent of the SNR.

C.4. Energy Consumption of a GEMV

Reading the seven terms at unit block sizes. Substituting D=ND=N and Lw=Lx=L=1L_{w}=L_{x}=L=1 into the “Energy per module” column of Tab. A3 gives the “Energy per GEMV” column of Tab. A4, and dividing by the 2​M​N2MN FLOPs of the GEMV gives its “Energy per FLOP” column. Two terms are worth reading out at these block sizes. The ADC is charged for a single sample: the RF-mixer output has been low-pass filtered into a single-subcarrier bandwidth of Δ​f\Delta f, so one complex sample captures the outputs of the whole IP pair by its real and imaginary components. The FFT term vanishes with log2⁡L\log_{2}L, as the FFT that follows the ADC is trivial for its single sample per antenna.

Energy consumption scaling law. Summing the six remaining per-FLOP terms of Tab. A4 gives the energy per FLOP of AIR-LLM. Every term of this per-FLOP energy consumption is amortized by one of the dimensions as the GEMV scales up in LLM:

  • • Amortization over the input size NN: the ADC, postcoding, and summation terms scale as 1/N1/N, as one ADC sample squeezes the whole input dimension into a scalar, on which the postcoding and the summation are performed regardless of NN.
  • • Amortization over the output size MM: the precoding and IFFT terms scale as 1/M1/M, as the precoded waveform is stored and reused across all the rounds of a GEMV.
  • • Amortization over the antenna number AA: the DAC term scales as 1/A1/A, as its single waveform is fanned out to all the AA RF mixers.

Among the three, the DAC term is the bottleneck, since A≪N,MA\ll N,M in practice: it is amortized only by how many antennas an edge device can physically deploy, which massive MIMO keeps relieving as it scales up the array.

Appendix D AIR-LLM in CNN

Convolutional (CONV) layers, which dominate CNNs, do not fit the one-subcarrier-per-output mapping of the main body: reusing the same kernel across all I2I^{2} positions of an image would require re-transmitting that kernel once per output pixel, so the broadcast weight traffic, the very resource AIR-LLM is built to save, would grow by I2I^{2}. The BCO of Appendix B removes that restriction, as one mixing round now retains a whole output block instead of a single subcarrier, and a kernel broadcast once is correlated against every position of the image within it. We map a Conv2D layer onto the BCO (§D.1), and then specialize the BCO airtime of §C.1 and the BCO energy of §C.2 to it (§D.2 and §D.3).

D.1. Mapping Conv2D onto BCO

Layer formulation. We examine a general Conv2D layer with a kernel size of K×KK\times K, an image size of I×II\times I, NN input channels, and MM output channels, so that 𝐖(CONV)∈ℝN×M×K×K\mathbf{W}^{\textrm{(CONV)}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M\times K\times K}, 𝐗(CONV)∈ℝN×I×I\mathbf{X}^{\textrm{(CONV)}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times I\times I}, and 𝐘(CONV)∈ℝM×I×I\mathbf{Y}^{\textrm{(CONV)}}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times I\times I}. We assume KK is odd and that the correlation is zero-padded to preserve the image size. Just as a GEMV decomposes into MM inner products, this Conv2D decomposes into MM independent sub-convolutions, one per output channel, each of which becomes one BCO; as the layer is real-valued whereas the BCO is complex-valued, two output channels are packed into the real and the imaginary parts of a single BCO, as the two IPs of (4) are.

Blocks as input channels, subcarriers as pixels. For each sub-convolution we set D=ND=N, letting one block correspond to one input channel, so that the block accumulation in (14) performs exactly the summation over input channels. To embed the 2D image correlation into the 1D BCO, we flatten the I×II\times I image row by row and pad each row with KK zeros, so that the correlation of one row does not leak into the next; this gives each row a slot of length I+KI+K, hence

(28) Lx=I⁡(I+K).\displaystyle L_{x}=I(I+K).

The kernel is flattened the same way, row by row, but each of its rows is instead padded with II zeros so that its row stride matches that of the flattened image, giving

(29) Lw=K⁡(I+K).\displaystyle L_{w}=K(I+K).

Following L=Lw+Lx−1L=L_{w}+L_{x}-1 and approximating away the −1-1, the output block length is

(30) L≈(I+K)2,\displaystyle L\approx(I+K)^{2},

out of which the I2I^{2} subcarriers sitting at the valid correlation lags carry 𝐘(CONV)\mathbf{Y}^{\textrm{(CONV)}} of this output channel, and the remainder are discarded together with the LPF-rejected slots. Repeating this over all MM output channels sweeps 𝐰m\mathbf{w}_{m} and 𝐲m\mathbf{y}_{m} while sharing the same 𝐱\mathbf{x}, exactly the structure the central radio broadcasts and the AA antennas consume in parallel, two output channels per antenna. Notably, the kernel is broadcast once for the whole image: the reuse of a kernel across positions is absorbed by the correlation itself rather than paid for in weight traffic.

Padding overhead. The MM BCOs nominally complete 2​N​M​K​I​(I+K)22NMKI(I+K)^{2} FLOPs, of which only 2​N​M​K2​I22NMK^{2}I^{2} are useful to the CONV layer; the rest are correlation taps created by the zero padding. We denote this inefficiency by the ratio of nominal to useful FLOPs,

(31) η=(I+K)2K​I≥1,\displaystyle\eta=\frac{(I+K)^{2}}{KI}\geq 1,

which approaches I/KI/K for I≫KI\gg K. All per-FLOP metrics below are reported per useful FLOP, i.e., scaled by η\eta, so that they are directly comparable with the GEMV results of the main body.

D.2. Airtime of Conv2D

Airtime per FLOP. Substituting (28)–(30) into the per-FLOP airtime of a general BCO in (24), and scaling by the padding overhead η\eta of (31), yields the airtime per useful FLOP of a Conv2D layer,

(32) τCONV∝η⋅LA​B​Lw​Lx=1A​B⋅(I+K)2K2​I2.\displaystyle\tau_{\textrm{CONV}}\propto\eta\cdot\frac{L}{ABL_{w}L_{x}}=\frac{1}{AB}\cdot\frac{(I+K)^{2}}{K^{2}I^{2}}.

Comparison against GEMV. Against the GEMV airtime τGEMV\tau_{\textrm{GEMV}} of (27), which shares the same proportionality constant, we have

(33) τCONVτGEMV=(I+K)2K2​I2→I≫K1K2.\displaystyle\frac{\tau_{\textrm{CONV}}}{\tau_{\textrm{GEMV}}}=\frac{(I+K)^{2}}{K^{2}I^{2}}\xrightarrow{~I\gg K~}\frac{1}{K^{2}}.

Interestingly, despite the padding inefficiency η\eta, a Conv2D layer is faster per useful FLOP than a GEMV, occupying up to K2×K^{2}\times less airtime. This is because the BCO’s block-wise correlation structure is intrinsically matched to the convolution’s reuse of one kernel across all positions of the image: a single OFDM symbol that carries K2K^{2} kernel taps produces I2I^{2} output pixels, whereas under the GEMV mapping the same symbol duration would produce only one.

D.3. Energy Consumption of Conv2D

Assuming I≫KI\gg K, so that Lx≈L≈I2L_{x}\approx L\approx I^{2} and Lw≈K​IL_{w}\approx KI in (28)–(30), and substituting the Conv2D mapping (D=ND=N) into the “Energy per module” column of Tab. A3 gives that of Tab. A5, and dividing by the 2​N​M​K2​I22NMK^{2}I^{2} useful FLOPs of the layer gives its “Energy per useful FLOP” column.

Takeaways. Two opposite trends are visible in Tab. A5. On the one hand, the ADC and the cross-unit-summation terms both carry 1/N1/N and vanish as the layer deepens, exactly as in the GEMV case of Tab. A4: one ADC sample and one cross-unit addition now serve an entire input channel of the image rather than a single weight element, which is the saving that the reduced output bandwidth B/DB/D buys and that the remote baseline cannot obtain. The DAC term likewise decays as 1/K21/K^{2}, mirroring the airtime gain of (33). On the other hand, the digital encoding and decoding terms do not cancel as cleanly. Each of them does carry an amortization of its own, the transmitter-side precoding and IFFT over MM and the receiver-side FFT and postcoding over NN, so all three dimensions of §C.4 survive the Conv2D mapping intact. What survives with them, however, is a logarithmic factor the GEMV mapping does not have: the IFFT over all N​I2NI^{2} subcarriers and the receive FFT over the I2I^{2} subcarriers of a block leave a residual log2⁡(N​I)\log_{2}(NI) and log2⁡I\log_{2}I that both grow with the image size. Consequently, unlike the airtime of §D.2, where a larger kernel or image is strictly beneficial, the energy of Conv2D trades the analog savings on the converters against the digital cost of the wider OFDM symbol, and the two must be weighed together when choosing AIR-LLM’s operating point.

Appendix E Experimental Setup

This section details the baselines, the tasks, and the metrics of the evaluation, together with the two measurements that the implementation of §4 rests on: the distortion profile of the RF mixer (Fig. A2) and the path-loss distribution of each ray-traced scene (Fig. A3).

E.1. Measured Distortion and Path Loss

Distortion profile of the RF mixer. Fig. A2 reports the wired sweep of §4: at each power delivered to the mixer’s RF port, the LO power is swept and the best ENOB is kept. The ENOB climbs with the RF power and then flattens as the mixer’s own nonlinearity takes over from the drive level; this knee is the distortion floor that the saturated users of §5.3 sit on.

Path loss across the candidate devices. Fig. A3 shows the PL distribution of the 100 candidate devices dropped in each scene, from which the representative devices of §5.1 are selected. The open scene of Paris is tightly concentrated, a single mode of median 84.0 dB with 5/95-th percentiles of 74.9/97.8 dB, since almost every drop keeps an LOS path to the central radio. The dense scene of Munich is both worse and far wider, a median of 91.4 dB and percentiles of 75.2/131.3 dB, with a long shadowed tail of devices whose LOS path is blocked by a building. Both scenes therefore span the range of link qualities from the noise-limited users of §5.3 to the distortion-limited ones.

E.2. Baselines

We benchmark AIR-LLM against digital baselines along two dimensions: the precision at which the weights are kept, and the weight storage from which they reach the edge device.

Precision dimension. We take FP16 as the exact reference, and further consider weight-only quantization (WoQ) at 4/3 bit, i.e., W4A16 and W3A16, by RTN, GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023), and AWQ (Lin et al., 2024).

Analog computing baselines. We further benchmark against two analog computing baselines at the same ENOB as AIR-LLM’s device: (i) AWGN, additive Gaussian noise on each GEMV output, and (ii) HyFlexPIM, a multiplicative Gaussian error on each weight, i.e., the conductance spread of a memristive crossbar. The former error is redrawn per GEMV, whereas the latter is frozen on the weights; AIR-LLM sits in between, as its thermal noise is redrawn per transmission while its calibration residual and mixer distortion hold for as long as the channel does.

Weight storage dimension. Under remote storage, the weights are kept on the central radio and delivered to the edge device over the same wireless channel as AIR-LLM’s by a standard communication link. Under local storage, they are instead pre-stored in the edge device’s memory. AIR-LLM targets the remote storage, which is both more realistic for edge computing and more challenging than the local one.

E.3. Evaluation Tasks and Metrics

Benchmarking GEMV with ENOB. We first benchmark AIR-LLM on a single GEMV 𝐲=𝐖⋅𝐱\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{W}\cdot\mathbf{x}, whose weights 𝐖\mathbf{W} and inputs 𝐱\mathbf{x} are randomly drawn from i.i.d. Gaussian distributions, and quantify its computing accuracy by the effective number of bits (ENOB), defined as

(34) ENOB=−12⋅log2(𝔼𝐱,𝐖[1M∑m=0M−1|𝐲m−𝐲^m|2]),\displaystyle\textsf{ENOB}=-\frac{1}{2}\cdot\log_{2}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{W}}\left[\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}\left|\mathbf{y}_{m}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{m}\right|^{2}\right]\right),

where both the ground truth 𝐲\mathbf{y} and its estimate 𝐲^\hat{\mathbf{y}} are normalized by the standard deviation of 𝐲\mathbf{y}. A trivial estimate 𝐲^=𝟎\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{0} thus sits at exactly 0 bit.

PPL and zero-shot accuracy on LLM. We then run whole LLMs over AIR-LLM, including LLaMA-3.2 (1B and 3B) (Meta AI, 2024), LLaMA-3.1 (8B and 70B) (Grattafiori et al., 2024), LLaMA-2 (7B and 13B) (Touvron et al., 2023), Mistral-7B (Jiang et al., 2023), and Gemma-4 (E2B and E4B) (Gemma Team, 2026), where every weight-activation GEMV is performed by AIR-LLM’s RF computing and the rest stays digital. We report (i) the PPL on WikiText-2 (Merity et al., 2017) and (ii) the zero-shot accuracy on PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), ARC-e and ARC-c (Clark et al., 2018), BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), and WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2020).

Airtime and energy consumption. We further report the airtime and the energy consumption per token. The airtime is the time one token occupies the wireless link, the resource the central radio rations across the edge devices it serves; for the remote storage baselines, it is counted on the same ray-traced channel under a standard-compliant 5G NR link (3GPP, 2022a; 3GPP, 2022b), while the local storage baselines occupy no airtime. The energy consumption is based on the per-operation energies of state-of-the-art DACs (Olieman et al., 2015), ADCs (Harpe et al., 2011; Murmann, 2026), digital computing (NVIDIA, 2024), and data movement (Antepara et al., 2025).

F.2. Benchmarking on LLM

Energy and airtime per token in Munich. Fig. A5 repeats Figs. 8 and 9 on the selected device of Munich, whose roughly 3 bit of end-to-end resolution reads it against the W3A16 baselines. The energy conclusion of §5.2 carries over unchanged: on LLaMA-3.1-8B, AIR-LLM costs 165.5×\times and 32.1×\times less energy than the remote FP16 and W3A16 baselines, and 51.5×\times and 10.7×\times less than the two local ones, holding at 28.3–35.3×\times and 10.0–11.1×\times against the two W3A16 baselines over all nine LLMs. That the gain against the local FP16 baseline is exactly the 51.5×\times of Paris is no coincidence: AIR-LLM’s per-token energy is set by its own DAC, digital pipeline, and unit number, none of which depends on the channel, and a local baseline pays data movement rather than airtime, so neither side of that ratio moves with the scene. The airtime does move, and it moves in AIR-LLM’s favor: the remote FP16 baseline takes 5.37–5.42×\times AIR-LLM’s airtime here against 5.11×\times in Paris, since the worse link costs the communication baseline capacity while AIR-LLM’s signal duration is fixed by BB and AA alone (27). The quantized baseline, in contrast, closes to 1.01–1.02×\times from the 1.28×\times that W4A16 leaves in Paris: a quarter fewer bits per weight is enough to offset the capacity its own link costs it.

What each edge device generates. Fig. A6 and Tabs. A6 and A7 put the PPLs of §5.4 next to what the model actually writes: each of the 20 devices per scene continues one shared prompt, with every GEMV of LLaMA-3.1-8B carried over that device’s own ray-traced channel. The rows fall by ENOB, and the degradation along them is graded rather than abrupt. Above about 3.5 bit, which 16 of the 20 devices reach in Paris and 8 in Munich, the continuations are fluent and name the city’s real landmarks, differing from the FP16 reference in which true fact they pick rather than in whether they pick one at all. Below it they stay grammatical but drift into invented detail and begin to repeat themselves, e.g., device 3 of Paris at 3.21 bit dates a fountain to 1772 and device 11 of Munich at 3.16 bit loops on its beer gardens, while their PPLs are still only 7.99 and 7.27. Only under about 2.5 bit do they collapse: device 18 of Paris restarts the prompt verbatim at 2.52 bit, device 4 of Munich does the same at 2.49 bit, and device 11 of Paris, the near-singular channel of §5.4, degenerates into repeated tokens at 2.00 bit and the outlying PPL of 255.27. This is the practical reading of the CDFs in Fig. 11: AIR-LLM degrades an LLM gracefully over most of a coverage zone, and the devices it fails are the few whose channel is too poorly conditioned to invert rather than the ones that are merely far away: device 12 of Munich, the most distant of all 40 at 105.0 dB, still resolves 4.19 bit and reads a PPL of 6.60.

Zero-shot accuracy using LLaMA-3.1-8B. We evaluate AIR-LLM and the same set of baselines on LLaMA-3.1-8B’s inference on six commonsense-reasoning benchmarks, as shown in Tab. A8. This metric is harsher on analog computing than the PPL, because of how it is scored: every candidate continuation is concatenated to the same stem and run through its own inference pass, and the answer is the candidate with the highest log-likelihood. An error that is deterministic given the weights, the quantization grid of WoQ or the frozen conductance spread of HyFlexPIM, shifts all the candidates of a question in the same direction, so the comparison among them, and thus the argmax, largely survives. A non-deterministic one does not: the AWGN baseline and AIR-LLM’s thermal noise are redrawn independently in every pass, so each candidate is scored under its own realization of the error, and the choice flips whenever that perturbation exceeds the log-likelihood margin between the candidates. AWGN pays for this in full, collapsing to the chance level on all six tasks (37.98% at ENOB 4 and 36.30% at ENOB 3) despite an ENOB matched to AIR-LLM’s, whereas the weight-frozen HyFlexPIM stays within 0.42 points of the FP16 reference at ENOB 4. AIR-LLM sits between the two, averaging 68.72% in Paris and 65.67% in Munich against the 75.00% FP16 reference, as only its thermal noise is redrawn per transmission while its channel-calibration residual and the mixer’s distortion hold across the candidates of a question: Paris sits inside the W3A16 band (66.00–69.96%) and Munich 0.33 points below its weakest member. Task by task, the degradation is mild where the margins between the candidate continuations are wide (77.85%/75.39% on HellaSwag against 78.89%, and 81.13%/75.20% on BoolQ against 81.96%), and the average is dominated by WinoGrande (57.77%/57.14% against 73.56%), whose two candidates differ in a single pronoun referent and whose log-likelihood margin is therefore the narrowest of the six, so a few bits of analog error are enough to flip the choice.

F.3. Impact of the System Factors

Impact of repeating the weight signal. The central radio may send the same weight signal several times and let the edge device average the copies, which trades airtime for a lower thermal noise: repeating it nn times costs nn times the airtime and lowers the noise power by 10​log10​n10\log_{10}n dB, while leaving the receive chain’s own distortion untouched. Tab. A9 sweeps this knob under the same LLaMA-3.1-8B setup as Tab. 4, where the last column measures the distortion floor that no repetition count can pass. The Paris user does not move at all, staying at 6.49 from a single copy to the floor, which confirms the same conclusion as its flat row in Tab. 4: this user is already limited by the channel calibration and the RF mixer rather than by the noise. The noise-limited Munich user does improve, but slowly: 16 copies, i.e., 16 times the airtime, buy 7.37 to 7.19, only 2.4% and already within 0.3% of its 7.17 floor. Repetition is therefore a much worse deal than the transmit power for the same user, which buys 7.9% over the same 10 dB in Tab. 4 at no airtime cost, and we keep a single copy of the weight signal throughout the other evaluations.

Impact of the carrier frequency. We repeat the transmit power sweep of Tab. 4 in two other bands, the 915 MHz ISM band over 25 MHz and the 28 GHz mmWave band over 400 MHz, on the same two edge devices at the same positions and under the same LLaMA-3.1-8B setup, as shown in Tab. A10. The channels are re-traced at each carrier with the same scenes, whose ITU-R P.2040 material models are extrapolated below their 1 GHz lower edge for 915 MHz, and the noise floor follows the bandwidth of each band. Since the path loss of the two devices drops by 12 dB at 915 MHz and grows by 32 dB (Paris) and 41 dB (Munich) at 28 GHz, the power axis is shifted accordingly, with the regulatory ceilings of 36 dBm EIRP in the ISM band and 75 dBm per 100 MHz at 28 GHz inside the swept range. In the ISM band, both devices reach the accuracy of the paper’s operating point at 20 dB less power: Munich reads 7.28 at 30 dBm against the 7.37 that Tab. 4 measures at 50 dBm, while Paris has already saturated at 6.72. Both therefore stay usable inside the regulatory ceiling, reading 6.70 and 6.74 at 35 dBm, and the band’s own floors (6.69 in Paris and 6.44 in Munich) even reverse the two devices’ order, the lower carrier reaching the more distant device better than the nearer one. What the band costs is airtime: its 25 MHz is a quarter of the bandwidth BB that (26) divides, so every GEMV occupies four times the air.

At 28 GHz the trade reverses. Paris needs 80 dBm to saturate, 30 dB more than at 3.5 GHz, and saturates 9% worse, at a floor of 7.05 against 6.48; this gap is a distortion floor that no transmit power removes, the sparser multipath of the band leaving each per-subcarrier channel matrix worse conditioned for the calibration units to invert. Munich, another 17 dB of path loss away (a gap the band itself widens, from 7.9 dB at 3.5 GHz to 16.7 dB here), never becomes usable at all: 170.87 at the regulatory ceiling and still 9.98 at 100 dBm, i.e., 19 dB beyond what the band is allowed to radiate. Its 400 MHz does cut the airtime fourfold, but only for a device close enough to the central radio to spend it. Across the three bands, therefore, the carrier frequency trades airtime against coverage almost one for one, and AIR-LLM is the more comfortable the lower the band, the opposite of where the spectrum for it is easiest to find.

Each block is read at the transmit power where its own band saturates these devices, taken off Tab. A10 rather than carried over from the 3.5 GHz table, so that the unit count is again the only quantity the table varies: 30 dBm at A=4A={4} and 40 dBm at A=8A={8} in the ISM band, and 80 dBm and 90 dBm at 28 GHz, each following the same +10+{10} dB step between the two antenna blocks that the 3.5 GHz table uses.
